summary: Design a start-from-zero fundamentals primer track for DEREF (concepts before problems), beginner-empathy checked, then sequenced into a curriculum + Guided-Tour mode spec

jargon: "ops" in the STEPS(ops) meter, and more fundamentally what a "step" even IS and why anyone counts them — the whole payoff hinges on this meter but it's never explained that a step = a unit of work and fewer = faster.

The `nums[3]` / `nums[i]` square-bracket notation (and the name `nums`) — it appears cold in the commonBeginnerConfusion section and the code card, but the tour only ever talks about crates/boxes and never bridges 'the crate at index 3' to the actual syntax `nums[3]`.
"address" (analogy) — used as a plain synonym for the painted number, but 'address' is itself a loaded term the beginner hasn't met; borderline but leans on future jargon.
"N" in 'N identical crates' — mathematical shorthand for 'some count,' unexplained to a non-math reader.
"indices" (in 'valid indices are 0,1,2,3,4') — the plural of index may read as a brand-new word to a beginner who just learned 'index.'

"position = number × crate-width" (shown on screen per clientVisual): "crate-width" is never explained and is irrelevant to the concept; worse, it overloads the word "position" — earlier "position" means the index (a slot number), here it means a pixel x-coordinate. Two meanings, one word.

"index" / 0-based counting: leaned on throughout ("tape[0]", "crate labeled 0", "biggest index") and grounded via crate labels, but never restated in plain words in-body as "the crate's number, and we start counting at 0." A lost beginner will wonder why the far-left crate is 0 and not 1.

"traversal" and "auto-increments" (in feedsInto teaser): new terms; glossed inline but "traversal" as a label still lands before its plain-English meaning if surfaced on screen. Body wisely says "add one / subtract one" then switches to "auto-increment" here — inconsistent register.
tape[i] bracket notation: the aha rests entirely on the learner already reading nums[i] fluently (declared prereq array-indexing), which the profile says he has NOT internalised.

"Big-O" itself: the primer teaches the FEELING of growth beautifully but never once shows the actual symbol (O(n), O(n²)). A concept literally named "bigo" that never connects the felt gap to the notation the learner will meet in every interview/doc/tutorial leaves them able to feel it but unable to NAME it. He'll watch this, get the aha, then see "O(n²)" elsewhere and not realize it's the same thing he just held in his hands.

"comparing" (SLOW lane): the robot R "compares L's crate against each other crate" — but this is billed as a pure no-problem tour, so a beginner immediately asks "comparing to find WHAT?" and there's no answer given. The word smuggles in a hidden task and can stall him on a question the tour deliberately refuses to answer yet.

"work" (in the definition): the opening sentence hangs the whole idea on "amount of work," but "work" isn't grounded until the op-meter is defined several beats later. On first read "work" is abstract — a beginner can't tell if it means keystrokes, seconds, memory, or lines of code.

"binary search" and "two-pointer" — dropped inside the MECHANISM ("Binary search and two-pointer are nothing more than clever ways of always standing where...") before they're ever taught. Reading that, a lost beginner thinks "I'm supposed to already recognise these" and feels behind. They belong in feedsInto (where they're fine); the flaw is naming them mid-explanation as if known.

"op meter" / "op" — the abbreviation "op" (operation) is never spelled out. It's semi-self-explaining ("clicks up... for every crate it inspects"), but it also clashes with the on-screen tally the clientVisual calls "crates checked" — so the narration and the actual UI label use two different words for the exact same thing, which beginners anchor hard on.

"the atom" ("one comparison erasing a whole region — is the atom") — used metaphorically to mean "the fundamental unit," but a beginner reads the literal science word and stalls. Needs a four-word gloss.

"tape" / "crates" / "pointer-robot" — the entire explanation rides on this metaphor but it is never re-stated inside this doc; it relies wholly on the prereq levels having been done and remembered. No one-line reminder is given.
"≤" / "≥" — a Python dev knows the symbols, but for someone described as "genuinely easily lost" they should be said in words the first time ("≤ 4, i.e. 4 or smaller").

"hash" / "hashing" — the concept's own name, baked into hash map / hash set / hash gadget, is used purely as a label and never defined; the learner never finds out that "to hash" means "run a value through the rule to get its slot number."
"address" — appears only in theOneAha ("computes its own address"); the entire mechanism says "slot"/"hole," so "address" reads like a newly introduced term rather than a synonym.

"array" — appears in the concept title and the confusion section but is never glossed in-primer; it's also silently swapped in for "list"/"tape"/"board", so the beginner can't tell they're the same object
"target" — used from the mechanism onward and in trivialHandsOn ("no target, no goal") but only ever implied via the analogy, never plainly defined as "the number you're aiming for"
"converged" — mechanism says "the robots have converged on the pair"; a beginner may not know the word (say "met")
"single left-to-right sweep" — in theOneAha; not only unexplained but inaccurate (the markers close in from both ends)

O(n) / O(n²) / "brute-force" / "one pass" / "linear" — used in feedsInto; design-facing here, but this vocabulary must not leak into the Tour narration and must be glossed when it first appears in the later problem level
"28 pairs" — the check-everything baseline number is dropped without saying where it comes from (8 crates paired with every other = 28)

O(n) and O(n^2): dropped naked in commonBeginnerConfusion and feedsInto, never defined, not in prereqs. Biggest glaze-over moment for a true beginner, and painful because the STEPS-vs-RECOMPUTE meters already teach this idea visually before the text throws it away in symbols.
'invariant' (step 5): explained inline right after, but the word itself is never defined and is intimidating to lead with.
'ops' (in 'STEPS (ops) meter'): never spelled out as 'operations'; the whole lesson hinges on ops=work.
'index 0' (step 1): assumes array-indexing vocabulary; a Python user likely survives it but it is used before it is grounded.
'substring' (feedsInto): appears with no gloss, lower-stakes as a forward pointer.
'running number/value' (plainDefinition): 'running' meaning kept-up-to-date is colloquial and never unpacked.

'queue' — named in commonBeginnerConfusion as 'a completely different structure' but never given even a one-line what-it-is; the everyday 'line of people' meaning carries it, yet calling it a *structure* dangles a forward reference a beginner can't cash

append() as the Python name for PUSH — pop() maps to POP by sound, but PUSH and append() share no letters and the prose never states 'PUSH is append()'; the link lives only in the code-card visual, so a reader following the text alone can miss it

"log time" — the felt intuition is given ("double the haystack, pay one more guess"), but the word "log" is dropped as if the reader already connects it to logarithms/Big-O. A true beginner won't link this to the "O(log n)" he'll meet the moment he opens LeetCode 704.

"the two-pointer view" — the clientVisual and mechanism reuse the L/R robots "from the two-pointer view," assuming he's already played a prior two-pointer tour. Played standalone, this is a dangling reference to a concept never introduced here.

"sorted" — used as THE load-bearing precondition (the whole confusion section hinges on it), yet never defined in one plain line. It's a common word, but given how much weight it carries, a beginner shouldn't have to infer that "sorted" means each crate is >= the one before it.

"(L+R)//2" / midpoint — the formula is shown but never called out as recomputing on the *shrinking window*, not the fixed tape. A beginner can easily miss that the middle moves relative to L and R each step.
"leaf" (in feedsInto: "hitting a dead-end or a leaf is the base case") — tree terminology dropped with zero explanation; a beginner has no picture for it.
"frame" / "active-frame" (clientVisual: "a single active-frame robot") — stack-frame jargon used raw; nowhere is it said that a frame = one crate = one paused copy.
"PC" (clientVisual: "call it PC") — labeled but never unpacked; "program counter" is never spelled out, only its behavior is hinted.

"LIFO" (prereqs: "stack-lifo-column") — acronym never expanded; if this label is ever shown to the learner it's opaque. (The primer DOES explain the idea plainly as "cleared away one at a time from the top down," so fix by never surfacing the acronym.)
"tree" / "maze" as data structures (feedsInto) — used as if familiar; acceptable since it's forward-looking, but still asserted, not shown.

"node" — the highlighted code line `node = node.left` is shown on screen (clientVisual), but the entire primer calls these things "boxes" and never once says a box is called a node in code. This is the single most jarring gap: he's told "box" everywhere, then the code panel he's supposed to watch uses a word he was never given.

"tree" vs "binary tree" — the primer defines a tree as "up to two strings" and presents that as THE definition, but that's actually a *binary* tree. The word "binary" only appears later in feedsInto ("Binary Search Tree"), unexplained, and he's never told other trees can have more than two children. He'll form the misconception that all trees are 2-child.

"space_hi" — the on-screen depth meter label is cryptic. The design note explains it means "how deep the robot hangs below root," but that plain-English gloss isn't given as the visible caption, so the label itself teaches him nothing.

"box.left" vs "node.left" — Step 4 narration writes `box.left` while the code panel writes `node.left`. Two different tokens for the same move; a beginner matching narration to the highlighted line won't see them line up.

"BFS" / "DFS" — used ~a dozen times as bare labels and NEVER expanded to Breadth-First Search / Depth-First Search. To this beginner they're just opaque two-letter names; he's never told what the letters mean, so he can't feel that the name literally describes the behavior.

"traversal" / "tree traversal" — appears in commonBeginnerConfusion ("why tree traversal felt simpler") with no definition, AND it assumes he's already traversed trees and formed an opinion. He may never have.
"flood fill" — dropped in feedsInto as an alias for Number of Islands; only loosely inferable from the surrounding sentence.

"edges" — clientVisual introduces "edges = glowing wires" as the technical term, but the whole body only ever says "wires." A tooltip or panel derived from clientVisual would show him "edge" cold, without flagging it's the same thing as a wire.

"graph" — redefined immediately as dots-and-lines (good), but it never kills the everyday/math-class reflex that a "graph" is a bar chart or an x-y plot, which is exactly where a true beginner's mind goes first.

primers.plainDefinition: An array is a fixed row of boxes sitting side by side, and each box holds one value. Every box also has a position number, called its index, that tells you where the box sits in the row — and if you know a box's number, you can grab what's inside it instantly.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: A row of identical lockers bolted to a wall. The row is a fixed length — nobody adds or removes lockers while you're using it. Each locker has a number painted on it, and because every locker is the exact same width and you know precisely where the first one starts, you can walk straight to locker #7 without opening, or even glancing at, lockers 0 through 6. The painted number is the locker's address; the coat hanging inside is its value — two completely different things.
primers.mechanism: Show it in three beats, each on its own tour frame with the STEPS(ops) meter visible. (1) Lay down the tape: N identical crates, the value printed big in each, the index printed small underneath — 0,1,2,3,... The narration says the row's length is locked for this whole tour: no crate is ever added or removed. (2) Reveal the secret the machine actually stores: NOT every crate's location, just ONE thing — where the front of the tape is (the left edge of crate 0). Drop a faint 'FRONT' marker there. (3) Read nums[3]: instead of the robot walking crate-by-crate, draw a dashed ruler from FRONT and let the robot compute front + 3 x (crate width) in a single stroke and LAND on crate 3 — the in-between crates never light up. The STEPS meter ticks +1. Now read nums[0] (STEPS +1) and nums[7] (STEPS +1): same cost every time, because each is one jump, not a walk. This also quietly explains zero: the index is literally 'how many crate-widths from the front,' so the first crate is 0 crates away → index 0, and the last valid crate is length−1 away.
primers.theOneAha: The index is not a name you memorize for each box — it's the distance from the front of the row. That single fact explains everything: counting starts at 0 because the first box is 0 boxes from the front, and grabbing box 500 costs exactly the same as grabbing box 0 (one instant jump, never a walk), because the number itself tells the machine where to land.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No goal, nothing to find. Just drag the reader robot along the tape and drop it on any crate you feel like — crate 0, crate 4, the very last one — and keep an eye on the STEPS(ops) meter. It clicks up by exactly 1 every single time, no matter how far down the row you jump. Then try to shove the robot one crate PAST the end: it thunks into a little wall and won't go — the row is a fixed length, and there's no crate out there to read. Poke, watch, get a feel for it.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Two tangles, both from the same root — mixing up a box's number with what's inside it. First: thinking nums[3] means 'the 3rd box.' It doesn't — because counting starts at 0, nums[3] is the 4th box, and in a row of 5 boxes the valid indices are 0,1,2,3,4, so the LAST box is nums[4] (length−1), and nums[5] is already off the end into the wall. Second: reading nums[3] and expecting to get 3 back. You get whatever value is sitting IN box 3, which could be 99 or −7. The index is the box's address; the value is its contents. DEREF keeps these visually separate: index small and gray underneath, value big and bright inside.
primers.feedsInto: The linear scan (array traversal): walking the reader robot across every crate exactly once to compute or find something — the running SUM of the row, or the largest value, or 'is the number 42 in here anywhere?' It's the first real problem because it turns instant single-box access into 'visit them all in order,' and it's the seed the two-pointer patterns (like Two Sum) later grow from — once you're comfortable moving one robot across the tape, DEREF introduces a second robot.
primers.clientVisual: Reuse the existing substrate verbatim: the `_TapePainter` crates with the value drawn big/bright (`_ink`) and the index drawn small/gray (`_muted`) beneath each — no new metaphor needed, indices are already there. For the tour, drop the amber 'sortedness' gradient (it's meaningless here) so crates read as plain identical lockers, and use a SINGLE robot — the teal `L` caret relabeled 'READER' — instead of two. Add three tour-only overlays on the same tape card: a faint 'FRONT' tick at crate 0's left edge; a dashed measuring ruler from FRONT to the target crate that appears the instant you jump (index = number of crate-widths); and a small bumper 'wall' past the last crate for the out-of-bounds thunk. Keep the real `STEPS (ops)` stat tile front-and-center — it's the proof that every read is +1 — and gray out `SUM`/`AUX SPACE`/`POWER` since the tour computes nothing. Drive the beats with the existing scrubber and frame counter, and show a one-line code card, `x = nums[i]`, with the active line highlighted in teal exactly as the player already does. Narration rides in a caption bubble above the tape. All in the current dark machine-shop palette.

primers.plainDefinition: A pointer (also called a cursor) is just a bookmark: a little marker that remembers WHICH slot you're currently looking at. It doesn't hold the data itself — it holds a position, and that position is just a number.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: Your finger sliding under the word you're reading. Your finger isn't the word — it just remembers where you are on the line. To move to the next word, you don't rewrite the sentence; you just scoot your finger over one. The sentence stays exactly where it was; only your finger's spot changed. A bookmark in a book works the same way: it never contains a page, it only marks which page number you're on.
primers.mechanism:
Shown as a live trace on one tape of numbered crates (values 5, 8, 90, 2), with a single teal robot "L".

1) Start: L is holding the number 0. On screen the robot sits on the crate labeled 0 (far left) — because its position is literally index x crate-width, and 0 x width = far left. A readout tile shows "L = 0" and a second tile shows "points at tape[0] = 5".
2) Poke the [+1] button. Exactly ONE thing happens in the data: L = L + 1, so the stored number goes 0 -> 1. No crate moves. No value changes. Nothing else is touched.
3) The picture simply reacts to that one number: position is now 1 x crate-width, so the robot glides one crate right (the 550ms easeInOutCubic slide). Readout updates to "L = 1", "points at tape[1] = 8".
4) Poke [+1] again -> L becomes 2, robot slides to crate 2, "points at tape[2] = 90". Poke [-1] -> L subtracts one back to 1, robot slides left.

That is the entire machine: the pointer is a stored number; "moving" it is arithmetic on that number (add one, subtract one, or set it to any crate's index); the robot you see is only a live drawing of that number.
primers.theOneAha: A pointer is not a thing that lives on the tape — it is just a number, like the variable `i` you already write in Python every day. When you type `nums[i]`, the `i` WAS a pointer the whole time; you just never called it that. So "moving a pointer" is not a special skill or a magic operation — it is plain arithmetic: `i = i + 1`. The robot sliding across the crates is nothing more than a picture of that one number ticking up.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No goal, nothing to solve — just poke it. Drag the teal "L" robot with your finger and watch the number under it tick 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 as it hops from crate to crate. Or tap [+1] a few times and watch two things move together: the big readout flips "L = 1" to "L = 2", and the robot glides one crate right — every single time, in lockstep. Then tap any crate directly and watch L teleport there, the readout instantly showing that crate's index. Finally, spam [+1] past the last crate and notice it just parks on the biggest index and won't fall off — because it's only a number, not a real thing that can tumble off the edge. That's the whole point: you're not moving data, you're only changing a number, and the robot is just showing you that number.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Mixing up WHERE the pointer is with WHAT it's pointing at. When L = 2 and crate 2 holds the value 90, beginners say "the pointer is 90." No — the pointer's value is 2 (the position/index); 90 is the content sitting at that position (tape[2]). The primer keeps these on two separate readout tiles side by side ("L = 2" vs "points at tape[2] = 90") precisely so the split is impossible to miss. In Python terms: `i` is the pointer (a position), `nums[i]` is the thing it points at (the value) — two different numbers that beginners collapse into one.
primers.feedsInto: Once "a pointer is just a number you nudge," two things unlock. First, the plain traversal: a Python `for i in range(len(nums))` loop is secretly ONE pointer that auto-increments by 1 each pass — so scanning an array is just a pointer walking right on its own. Second, and this is the first real technique it opens: the two-pointer pattern — two cursors, L starting at index 0 and R at the last index, each step nudging one number toward the other until they meet. That is exactly DEREF's shipped "rendezvous" demo (Two Sum on a sorted array): every move there is just L = L + 1 or R = R - 1 on the numbers you now understand.
primers.clientVisual: Reuses the existing widgets almost as-is. The tape is the current `_TapePainter` crates, and we lean on a detail already drawn: the muted index label at the bottom of every crate (`$i`) — the tour highlights those so the learner ties "robot position" to "a number on the crate." The pointer is the existing teal "L" caret (arrow_drop_up + "L" chip) driven by `AnimatedPositioned` (550ms easeInOutCubic), so each move reads as one clean hop; its `left: index * cw` is called out on screen as "position = number x crate-width." In the meter row we repurpose two `_stat` tiles into "POINTER L = 2" and "POINTS AT tape[2] = 90" (attacking the position-vs-content confusion directly), and we dim/hide the SUM, AUX-SPACE, and POWER meters plus the amber sortedness gradient since none are relevant here — pure signal. The play/scrubber controls are swapped for a simple [-1] / [+1] stepper (still the same control row), and optionally a single ghosted code line `L = L + 1` in the reused `_codeCard` that flashes its teal active-line highlight on each poke, so the learner literally sees the arithmetic that the glide represents. R (magenta) stays offstage until the two-pointer primer.

primers.plainDefinition: Big-O is a way of describing how the AMOUNT OF WORK a program does grows as the pile of data it handles gets bigger. It is not a stopwatch measuring seconds — it is the shape of the growth: does the work rise gently, in step with the pile ("fast"), or blow up much faster than the pile ("slow")?
primers.realWorldAnalogy: Two ways to deal with a room full of people. (1) Roll call: you read each name once to see who showed up — 30 people, 30 checks; 60 people, 60 checks. Twice the people, twice the work, no drama. (2) Everyone shakes everyone else's hand: with 30 people that is already hundreds of handshakes; go to 60 and it is not double, it is roughly FOUR times as many. Same room, but adding people barely bothers the roll call and completely swamps the handshakes. "Fast" is the roll call. "Slow" is the handshakes.
primers.mechanism: DEREF puts the SAME tape of numbered crates in front of you twice, stacked, and gives each copy its own op meter (the counter that clicks up by 1 every time a robot touches a crate). FAST lane ("touch each once"): one robot starts on the leftmost crate and steps right, one crate at a time, to the end. Each step is one click. 10 crates -> the meter lands on 10. You literally watch it walk the tape exactly once and stop. SLOW lane ("check every pair"): robot L parks on the first crate; robot R sweeps the WHOLE tape past it, comparing L's crate against each other crate — about 10 clicks. Then L advances one crate to the right and R sweeps the whole tape AGAIN — another ~10 clicks. L keeps inching forward; R re-sweeps every single time. 10 crates -> the meter grinds all the way up to about 100. Now the reveal: DEREF lets you grow the tape. Push it from 10 crates to 20. FAST's meter goes 10 -> 20 (it just doubled). SLOW's meter goes ~100 -> ~400 (it quadrupled). The extra work you paid is not the same in the two lanes — the meters are pulling apart, and they pull apart harder the longer the tape gets.
primers.theOneAha: Big-O is NOT the number sitting on the op meter right now — it is how that number STRETCHES when you make the tape longer. "Touch each once" stretches like a rubber band (double the tape, double the work). "Check every pair" stretches like an explosion (double the tape, four times the work). The whole lesson lives in the growth, not in any single reading.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No puzzle, nothing to solve, nothing to get right. There is just a slider labeled n = how many crates are on the tape. Drag it: 5... 10... 50... 200, and watch the two op meters side by side. At n=5 they sit almost on top of each other (5 vs 25 — who cares, both blink instantly). Keep dragging and the SLOW meter tears off the top of the screen while the FAST meter barely creeps upward. You are not calculating anything — you are just feeling the gap yawn open as n gets big. Slide it back down and watch the gap close again.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Beginners assume Big-O measures TIME in seconds, and that "slow" (check-every-pair) is always worse than "fast" (touch-each-once). Neither is quite right. Big-O measures how the work GROWS, not how many milliseconds your laptop takes today — and when n is tiny (5, 10, 50 crates) the "slow" version is often perfectly fine, sometimes even quicker. It only turns into a disaster when n gets big, which is exactly why the slider matters. Second trap: mixing up n (how MANY crates there are) with the numbers written ON the crates. Big-O cares about the count of crates, never their values.
primers.feedsInto: Two Sum — but reached as a STORY instead of a trick. The obvious first solution parks one robot on a crate and sweeps a second robot across every other crate hunting for a matching pair — that is precisely the "check every pair" SLOW pattern the learner just felt in their hands. Having played this primer, Two Sum lands as "how do we collapse that check-every-pair work into a single touch-each-once pass?" — a motivated question — rather than a pattern you are somehow expected to already know.
primers.clientVisual: Split the stage into two stacked lanes showing the SAME tape of numbered crates. Top lane = FAST: one pointer-robot walks left-to-right exactly once, its op meter ticking +1 per crate, then it parks at the end. Bottom lane = SLOW: robot L parks on a crate while robot R sweeps the entire tape past it, then L advances one crate and R re-sweeps from the start — the meter climbing once per pair. Above both lanes sits a big n-slider that stretches or shrinks the shared tape live (crates slide in/out). Beside the meters, a small "growth graph" plots each meter's reading against n as you drag: FAST traces a nearly straight line, SLOW curves sharply upward and off the top. A "×2 the tape" button snaps the tape to double its length so you can watch FAST's meter roughly double while SLOW's roughly quadruples in the same beat. Everything reuses the existing crates, L/R pointer-robots, and op/step meter — plus the scrubber to replay a lane's sweep slowly — so zero new visual vocabulary is introduced.

primers.plainDefinition: Sorting just means putting the crates in order, smallest on the left, largest on the right. Once they're in order, looking at ONE crate quietly tells you something about ALL the others: everything to its left is smaller, everything to its right is bigger. So a single glance can let you throw away a whole chunk of the tape without ever checking it — and that's the thing that makes fast searching possible.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: A paper dictionary. Nobody hunting for "zebra" starts at page 1 and reads every word. You flop it open near the middle, see you've landed on "M", and instantly toss the entire first half — not because you checked those pages, but because alphabetical order PROMISES "zebra" can't be back there. Now picture a dictionary with the words shuffled into random order: that flip-and-toss move is impossible, and you're stuck reading every single page. Same book, same words — the only difference is order, and order is the whole game.
primers.mechanism:
Watch the same tape twice.

SHUFFLED run: The crates read [4, 9, 1, 7, 3, 8]. You're asking "where is 7?" A pointer-robot lands on the crate showing 4. Ask it: "does knowing this is 4 tell me anything about its neighbours?" No. The crate to its right could be 1, could be 99 — order gives no promise. So the robot has no choice but to shuffle right one crate at a time, and the op meter clicks up 1... 2... 3... for every crate it inspects. Worst case, it inspects all of them.

SORTED run: DEREF slides the very same crates into order: [1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9]. Now the robot lands on the crate showing 4. Ask again: "does knowing this is 4 tell me anything?" This time YES — because the tape climbs left to right, everything left of here is guaranteed ≤ 4 and everything right is guaranteed ≥ 4. You want 7, which is bigger than 4, so 7 (if it's anywhere) MUST be to the right. The moment that comparison happens, DEREF dims every crate from here leftward and drops a tag: "all ≤ 4 — 7 can't be here — skip." The robot never touches those crates. The op meter barely moves.

The step you just watched — one comparison erasing a whole region — is the atom. Binary search and two-pointer are nothing more than clever ways of always standing where that erase-a-region comparison pays off the most.
primers.theOneAha: In a sorted tape, one comparison isn't an answer about one crate — it's an answer about EVERY crate on one side of it. Order converts a single look into a whole region of "I already know." That leverage is the entire reason we bother sorting before we search.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No target, no goal, nothing to find. There's just the tape and one big toggle: SHUFFLED ⇄ SORTED. Drag the pointer-robot onto any crate you like and let go. On SHUFFLED, the crate you poked lights up but the rest of the tape stays fully lit, with a tiny caption: "the others could be anything." Flip to SORTED and poke the same crate: watch a grey curtain slide over the whole region that just became impossible, and a little "ruled out without looking: 3" counter tick up from zero. Poke around, flip the toggle back and forth, drag the robot to the far end and the far start. The only thing to notice is the feel: same poke, wildly different amount of the tape going dark. That difference IS what sorting buys you.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: "But how can you be SURE 7 isn't hiding on the left if the robot never looked over there?" This is the leap beginners resist — trusting a fact you derived instead of one you personally checked. The trust comes from the guarantee: sorted means the tape only ever climbs, so a crate showing 4 is a promise that nothing to its left exceeds 4, full stop. You're not skipping on a hunch; you're skipping on a rule the whole structure agreed to. (Related trap: thinking "sorted" means "solved." It doesn't — sorting is a setup move, like arranging your tools before the job. It's the precondition that makes the fast search legal, not the search itself.)
primers.feedsInto: Binary Search — the first real level where you deliberately stand in the MIDDLE of a sorted tape so that every single comparison erases half of what's left. Once "one look rules out a region" feels natural, that level stops looking like a memorized trick and starts looking obvious. From there it generalizes to the two-pointer Two Sum on a sorted array (robots L and R closing in from both ends, each move ruling out a row), which is the same leverage aimed from two sides at once.

Front and center: a SHUFFLED ⇄ SORTED toggle that, when flipped, plays a satisfying reshuffle — crates lift and slide into ascending order, cementing that "sorted" is a physical rearrangement of the very same values, not new data. Keep the scrubber available so a learner can rewind the reshuffle and the single ruling-out comparison and replay it as slowly as they want.

primers.plainDefinition: A hash map (Python's `dict`) or hash set (Python's `set`) is a big wall of labelled slots plus a tiny fixed rule that turns any value into the exact slot where it belongs. So instead of looking through everything to answer "is X in here?", you compute the one slot X would live in and jump straight to it.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: An old office mailroom: one wall of labelled pigeonholes, one slot per person. To check "did Ashish get mail?" you don't riffle through a single giant pile — you walk straight to the "Ashish" slot and look. The twist that makes it instant: the slot isn't found by searching, it's computed from the item itself. Like a coat check where your ticket number is derived from your coat — the attendant reads the number and walks straight to that one hook, never scanning the whole rack.
primers.mechanism:
Shown step by step, contrasting the tape you already know with the new wall:

1) THE PAIN (reuse the tape). Ask "have I seen 15?" on a tape of 8 crates. One robot walks left→right, reading each crate until it finds 15 or falls off the end. Worst case: 8 reads. The STEPS meter climbs 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Double the crates → double the walk. (This is "O(n)" — n meaning "how many items"; cost grows with the pile.)

2) NEW IDEA — let the value pick its own slot. Build a wall of numbered pigeonholes 0–9. Bolt a tiny fixed rule to its mouth, the "hash gadget": take the value, keep its last digit. 15→5, 23→3, 40→0. Any value in, one slot number out — and the SAME value always gives the SAME slot.

3) STORE. Drop 15 onto the gadget → it prints "5" → 15 flies in an arc straight into hole 5 (it does NOT walk the wall). Drop 23 → hole 3. Drop 8 → hole 8.

4) LOOK UP "have I seen 15?" Run 15 through the SAME gadget → "5" → peek in hole 5 only. 15 is there → yes. The STEPS meter reads exactly 1. It would still read 1 with a million values in the wall, because you never touch the other holes. (This is "O(1)" — one step, no matter the pile size.)

5) READ THE PRICE. To buy that instant jump you had to build the whole wall up front — including the empty holes. The AUX SPACE meter jumped the moment the wall appeared. That is the trade, made literal: you spent SPACE (the wall) to buy TIME (the one-step jump). "Trading space for time."

6) THIS IS JUST A PYTHON set/dict. `seen = set()` builds the wall; `seen.add(15)` runs the gadget and drops 15 in; `15 in seen` runs the gadget and peeks one hole. That is the entire trick.
primers.theOneAha: You never search a hash map — the value computes its own address. So "is X here?" costs the same single step whether the wall holds ten items or ten million. And the only reason it can is that you paid for the whole wall of slots up front: the instant answer is bought with space.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No goal, nothing to solve — just poke it. Grab the crate labelled 15 and drop it onto the hash gadget; watch the gadget flash "→ 5" and the crate skip straight into hole 5 while STEPS ticks to exactly 1. Now spin the "wall size" dial to stuff in 100, then 1000 more junk values — and watch the STEPS-for-a-lookup number refuse to move off 1, even as the AUX SPACE meter balloons. (Optional: drop that same 15 onto the OLD tape instead and watch the robot trudge crate-by-crate, STEPS climbing 1,2,3,4,5… Same question, two very different costs. You didn't answer anything — you just felt the difference.)
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Because both are written `x in ...`, beginners assume `x in my_list` and `x in my_set` cost the same. They don't. A list is the tape — Python walks it crate by crate, so cost grows with size. A set is the wall — Python computes the slot and peeks once, instant. Identical-looking syntax hides a completely different mechanism; the whole payoff lives in choosing `set`/`dict` over `list` for "have I seen it?" checks. (Second, smaller trap: "what if two values want the same hole?" — e.g. 15 and 25 both end in 5. The gadget isn't magic; the wall just keeps a tiny list inside that one hole, so it still works and stays effectively one step because crowding is rare. Beginners fear collisions break everything — they don't.)
primers.feedsInto: Contains Duplicate — literally this primer's question ("have I seen this value before?") turned into a real problem: walk the tape once, and before adding each value to the wall, ask the wall "seen you?" From there, Two Sum in a single pass: for each value x, ask the wall "have I seen target − x?". Both collapse from a slow item-times-item double-scan to a single walk, purely because the "have I seen it?" check is now free.

primers.concept: Two Pointers — the "squeeze" on a sorted array
primers.plainDefinition: You put one marker on the first item and one on the last item of a list that's already arranged small-to-big, then look at only that one pair. Because everything in between is in order, a single glance tells you which marker to step inward next — so you slide through the whole list once instead of trying every possible pair.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: A shelf of gym weights lined up light-on-the-left to heavy-on-the-right. You want two plates that together make exactly 17 kg. You put your left hand on the lightest plate and your right hand on the heaviest. Their sum is too heavy? The heavy end is the culprit, so your right hand slides one plate toward the middle — you don't bother with any plate it skips, because those were all even heavier. Too light? Your left hand steps up instead. Your two hands close in on each other until they either land on a 17 kg pair or bump into each other. You never had to weigh every combination — the ordering did the thinking for you.
primers.mechanism: Watched on the real board 2 3 5 8 11 15 19 24, target 17: (1) L-robot sits on crate 0 (value 2), R-robot on crate 7 (value 24). SUM meter reads 2+24 = 26. (2) Compare: 26 is BIGGER than 17. Ask "who's overshooting?" — the pair's biggest number is 24, on the right. Since every possible partner for 24 is at least 2, no pair using 24 can dip below 26. So 24 is hopeless: retire it. R-robot walks one crate left to crate 6 (value 19). STEPS meter ticks to 1. (3) SUM = 2+19 = 21, still bigger than 17 → same reasoning, retire 19 → R walks to crate 5 (value 15). STEPS = 2. (4) SUM = 2+15 = 17 — equal to target. The robots have converged on the pair; done. Notice the shape: every single step permanently retired exactly ONE end, so L and R can only march toward each other and are guaranteed to meet. Here it took 3 looks, not the 28 pairs a check-everything approach would need. (Mirror case: if the sum had been too SMALL, the LEFT end would be the one that's too weak to ever reach the target, so L advances right instead.)
primers.theOneAha: One comparison doesn't reject one pair — it wipes out a whole batch at once. The instant 2+24 came out too big, you didn't just rule out {2,24}; you simultaneously ruled out 24 paired with 3, 5, 8, 11, 15 and 19 too, because all of those partners are bigger than 2 and would only make the sum even bigger. One glance, an entire column of pairs gone forever. THAT is why a single left-to-right sweep is enough: sortedness converts "try every pair" into "eliminate one whole side per step."
primers.trivialHandsOn: No target, no goal, nothing graded — just grab the magenta R-robot with your finger and drag it. As it moves the SUM meter recomputes live under your hand. Slide R one crate to the left and watch SUM only ever go DOWN; slide it back right and watch it only ever go UP. Do the same with the teal L-robot. You're not solving anything — you're just feeling the thing that makes the whole trick work: on a sorted tape, moving a marker inward always changes the sum in one predictable direction. That "it only ever goes one way" feeling in your hand IS the squeeze, before any rule is ever stated.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Two tangled misreads. First: beginners think the robot carries the number, so dragging it drags the value along — it doesn't. The robot is just an eye pointing AT a crate; the crate values never move, you're only changing which two you're reading. Second: they think they get to CHOOSE which robot to step, or that they might guess wrong. You never choose — the comparison forces the move: sum too big means the right end is overshooting, so the right one is dragged inward; sum too small means the left end is too weak, so the left one advances. There's no guessing and no backtracking. And the deal-breaker to internalize: this only works BECAUSE the tape is sorted. On a shuffled tape "too big → shrink the right" is a lie, because a tiny number could be hiding at the right end — so the very first thing to check about any array is whether it's sorted.
primers.feedsInto: THE RENDEZVOUS level (Two Sum II): given a sorted array and a target, return the one pair of indices that adds up to it. After the tour, the squeeze IS the entire solution — the learner only has to supply the two forced moves (retire the right end when the sum is too big, advance the left end when it's too small) and watch the STEPS meter stay flat and linear (O(n), one pass) while the brute-force "check every pair" alternative browns out the POWER bar (O(n²)). The primer's intuition is now the algorithm, so the problem no longer feels like it appears from nowhere.

primers.plainDefinition: A sliding window is a stretchy frame you lay over a run of side-by-side crates on the array-tape. You slide it along the tape — letting a crate fall out the left edge and grabbing a new crate at the right edge — and instead of re-counting everything inside the frame every time it moves, you keep ONE running number and just nudge it up when a crate enters and down when a crate leaves.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: Picture a see-through picture-frame that covers three coins in a long row of coins on a table. You've added up the cash showing through the frame. Now you slide the frame one coin to the right. You do NOT recount all three coins — you just subtract the coin that slipped out the left side and add the coin that appeared on the right. One coin out, one coin in, and your total is correct again. The frame is the window; the total in your head is the running value; the only work per slide is the two coins at the edges.
primers.mechanism:
Watch it happen on the tape, one beat at a time — nothing is asserted, you see every number change:

1) START. Both robots stand under the same first crate (index 0). The window is one crate wide, and its glowing pane covers just that crate. The SUM meter reads exactly that crate's value, because that's all that's inside.

2) GROW (right edge). The R robot steps one crate to the right. That new crate is now inside the frame — so we ADD its value. Watch the entering crate flash green with a "+", the SUM meter jump by exactly that crate's number, and the STEPS (ops) meter tick up by just 1. Not "recount everything" — one single add.

3) Keep growing. Each further step of R = the pane stretches by one crate = one add = SUM rises by that one crate's value. The frame is now several crates wide but every move still cost only 1 op.

4) SHRINK (left edge). The L robot steps one crate to the right. The crate L just left is now OUTSIDE the frame — so we SUBTRACT its value. Watch the departing crate flash red with a "−", SUM drop by exactly that crate's number, STEPS tick up by 1 again.

5) The invariant you can literally read off the meters: the window is the crates from L to R inclusive (its width is R − L + 1), and the SUM meter ALWAYS equals the true total of exactly those crates — because every crate got added the moment it entered and subtracted the moment it left. Nothing double-counts, nothing is forgotten.

6) THE CONTRAST (this is the whole point). Flip on the grey RECOMPUTE ghost-meter — it shows what it would cost to re-add every crate inside the frame on each move. Slide the window across the tape and watch the two meters diverge: the ghost meter climbs fast (wider frame = more re-adding every step), while the real STEPS meter crawls up by 1 per move regardless of how wide the frame got. That growing gap is the payoff.
primers.theOneAha: The frame never re-counts what's inside it. Each slide, you only account for the ONE crate that entered and the ONE crate that left — so moving the window costs the same tiny two-nudge step whether the window is 3 crates wide or 3,000. The window remembers its total; you just correct it at the edges.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No goal, no target to hit — just poke the edges and watch the running number breathe. You're handed the tape with a glowing frame sitting over crates 0–2 and a live SUM meter. There are two buttons: "step R →" and "step L →". Tap "step R →": watch the pane stretch to swallow the next crate, that crate flash green, and SUM tick up by exactly its number while STEPS goes up by only 1. Now tap "step L →": watch the leftmost crate fall out of the frame, flash red, and SUM drop by exactly that crate's number. Tap them in any order you like. Optional: toggle the grey RECOMPUTE ghost-meter and keep tapping — feel the two meters drift apart. That's it. You're not solving anything; you're just learning that the total only ever changes by what crosses an edge.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: The big one: beginners assume the window is a brand-new sum every time it moves, so they mentally (and in code) re-add every element inside it on each step — a hidden inner loop that quietly turns the whole O(n) idea back into O(n²) work. The fix is the aha: you never rebuild the total, you only adjust it by the entering and leaving crate. Two smaller traps to name out loud: (a) forgetting the window is L..R *inclusive*, so its width is R − L + 1, not R − L; and (b) thinking every window is a fixed size — some windows keep a constant width (both robots step together), while others stretch and shrink at different times, but the add-on-enter / subtract-on-leave rule is identical for both.
primers.feedsInto: The gentlest first real problem: "the heaviest run of k crates" — given a fixed window width k, find the largest total among every run of k neighbouring crates. It's a one-pass slide across the tape: fill the first k-wide window, then slide it one crate at a time (add the entering crate, subtract the leaving crate), remembering the best SUM you ever saw. Because the total only nudges at the edges, the whole tape is swept in O(n). Once that clicks, it generalises straight into variable-width windows — e.g. "the shortest run of crates whose total reaches at least T" (grow R until you have enough, then shrink L to trim), which is the doorway to the classic "longest substring without repeating characters."

primers.plainDefinition: A stack is a container you're only allowed to touch at ONE end — the top. You add an item by dropping it on top, and the only item you can ever take out is the one sitting on top right now, which is always the last one you put in. That's the whole rule.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: A cafeteria plate dispenser: a spring-loaded tube of plates set into the counter. You push a clean plate down onto the pile and it sinks; the next person can only grab the plate on top — the one that was added most recently. Nobody can slide a plate out of the middle; the tube physically won't let them. That "you can only ever touch the top" fact IS a stack.
primers.mechanism:
A stack has exactly two moves, and no others:
- PUSH x — drop the value x onto the top of the pile.
- POP — remove the item currently on top and hand it back to you.

Watch one run, starting from an empty tube:
1) PUSH 3 → tube holds [3], top = 3.
2) PUSH 7 → 7 lands on 3, top = 7.
3) PUSH 9 → 9 lands on 7. Reading bottom-to-top the tube is 3, 7, 9; top = 9.
4) POP → it hands you 9 (the newest one). Tube is now 3, 7.
5) POP → it hands you 7. Tube is now 3.

Now notice what is MISSING: there is no "get the middle one" move and no "get the bottom one" move. To reach that first 3, you're forced to pop 9, then 7, first. The last thing you pushed is the first thing you get back — that behaviour has a name: LIFO, Last-In-First-Out. The absence of any middle-reaching move is not an oversight; it is the entire design.
primers.theOneAha: The restriction is not a weakness to work around — the restriction IS the feature. Because the only thing you can ever grab is the most-recently-added item, a stack automatically hands everything back in exact reverse order, newest first — for free, with zero bookkeeping. "Deal with the most recent thing, then unwind to the one before it" is precisely how Undo works, how the browser Back button works, and how "close the bracket you opened last" works. You don't tolerate a stack's one-end rule; you reach for a stack exactly WHEN you want that reversal.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No goal, nothing to solve — just poke it and watch. Drop three crates into the tube in order: 3, then 7, then 9, and watch each one settle on top of the one before it. Now press POP twice and watch which crate leaves each time — 9 comes out first, then 7 (newest first, always). Then try to click the bottom crate (the 3) to pull it straight out: the claw won't reach it — the crate just dims and gives a little refusing shake. Feeling that "no" in your hands is the whole point of a stack.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: The number-one trap: expecting the FIRST thing you added to come out first, the way people leave a queue in the order they arrived. A stack is the opposite. Push 3, 7, 9 and popping gives you 9, 7, 3 — reversed, not 3, 7, 9. (The "first-in-first-out" queue behaviour people intuitively imagine is a completely different structure.) Second trap for Python users: a list lets you index anywhere (mylist[1]), so it's tempting to peek into the middle — but the instant you do, it stops being a stack. A stack is the self-imposed discipline of only ever using append() and pop() at the end.
primers.feedsInto: Valid Parentheses: given a string like "([])", decide whether every bracket is properly closed. Nested brackets must close in the reverse order they were opened — the last one you opened is the first that has to close, which is pure LIFO. You push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket you pop the top and check it matches. It's the classic first stack problem, and the tube you just poked is exactly the machine that solves it — so the pattern will already feel obvious instead of being thrown at you cold.

primers.plainDefinition: Binary search is how you find something fast in a list that's already sorted. Instead of checking items one by one from the start, you look at the middle, ask "is what I want above or below this?", and throw away the entire half it can't be in. You repeat on what's left. Because you cut the leftovers in half every single time, even a list of a million items is found in about twenty looks.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: The "guess my number" game. A friend picks a number from 1 to 100 and after each guess says only "higher" or "lower." A beginner guesses 1, 2, 3... and might need 100 tries. The smart move: guess 50. "Higher" — and just like that, 1 through 50 are dead, gone, you'll never say them. Guess 75, "lower," now 51-74 is dead too. Every guess erases half the remaining possibilities, not one. Seven guesses covers all 100; you feel yourself closing in fast. (Same reason you flop a dictionary open in the middle to find "zebra" instead of reading from page one.)
primers.mechanism:
Watch it on a tape of 16 sorted crates, values [2,5,8,12,16,23,38,45,56,67,72,78,88,91,95,99] at indices 0..15. We're hunting the value 72. Two robots mark the window of crates that could still hold it: L on crate 0, R on crate 15. Everything between them is "still possible" and lit up.

Step 1: Land a MID robot at the middle, index (0+15)//2 = 7, which holds 45. Is 45 the target? No. Is 45 below 72? Yes. Since the tape is sorted, 72 cannot be anywhere at or left of crate 7 — so crates 0-7 go dark and are gone forever. L jumps to 8.

Step 2: Window is now 8..15. MID = (8+15)//2 = 11, holding 78. 78 is above 72, so 72 can't be at or right of crate 11 — crates 11-15 go dark. R jumps to 10.

Step 3: Window 8..10. MID = 9, holding 67. Below 72, so crates 8-9 go dark. L jumps to 10.

Step 4: Window 10..10. MID = 10, holding 72. Match. Found in 4 looks, on 16 crates (16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1). The only rule doing the work: each look compares the middle, then discards the half of the window that provably can't contain the answer.
primers.theOneAha: A guess doesn't remove ONE wrong answer — it removes HALF of everything still standing. So the number of guesses isn't tied to how big the list is; it's tied to how many times you can halve the list before one item is left. 16 halves to 1 in 4 steps. A thousand in ~10. A million in ~20. A billion in ~30. Double the haystack and you pay exactly ONE more guess. That's what "log time" feels like: the pile explodes, the work barely twitches.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No target to find, nothing to solve. There's one button: "×2". Press it and the tape doubles — 16 crates become 32, then 64, 128... keep hammering it until crates blur past a million and the tape scrolls off both edges. The whole time, watch the little "guesses needed" number beside the step meter. It doesn't double with the tape. It ticks up by exactly one: 5... 6... 7... 20. That single lazy tick against a flood of crates IS the felt idea. (Optional second poke: grab the MID robot and drop it anywhere off-center, then tap "too low"/"too high" yourself and watch which chunk of crates goes cold — the more centered your drop, the bigger the chunk that dies.)
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Two big ones. First, the shock: beginners expect a million items to take roughly a million steps — because their gut models search as "scan until you hit it," where each step kills one candidate. Binary search kills half per step, so the honest expectation is ~20, and that gap feels like a trick until you've watched the window collapse. Second, the silent killer: binary search ONLY works if the data is sorted. On an unsorted tape, "throw away the left half because the middle was too small" is a lie — the target could be sitting in the half you just deleted. It won't crash; it'll just confidently return the wrong answer. In DEREF the amber sortedness glow on the crates is the permission slip: no glow, no binary search.
primers.feedsInto: The classic first binary-search problem: given a sorted array and a target, return the index where it lives (LeetCode 704, "Binary Search"). Its close sibling comes right after — "Search Insert Position" (LeetCode 35): when the target is missing, instead of failing you return where it WOULD slot in, which turns out to be exactly the crate your L robot is parked on when the window closes. Both are the same machine the tour just built; the problem is only asking "what do you return at the end?"

Narration lines float above the tape ("45 is too low → the left half can't hold 72 → gone") instead of any prompt to solve.

primers.plainDefinition: Recursion is when a function does a big job by calling a fresh copy of itself to do a smaller version of the same job, then pausing until that copy hands back an answer. The "call stack" is just the pile of paused copies: each one is frozen mid-task, remembering where it was, and they get cleared away one at a time from the top down. The "base case" is the one rule that lets a copy answer instantly without calling another copy — it's the thing that stops the pile from growing forever.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: You're standing in a movie line and want to know how many people are ahead of you, but you can't see the front. So you tap the person in front: "How many are ahead of YOU? Add one for yourself and tell me." They can't see the front either, so they tap the person ahead of them and ask the exact same thing. This ripples forward. Every person is now frozen, holding one sticky note: "I still owe: their-answer + 1." The person at the very front has nobody ahead — that's the base case — so they say "zero" right away. Now "zero" flows back: each frozen person un-freezes, adds their +1, and passes the new number back to whoever tapped them. The chain of paused people IS the call stack: it builds forward as the question travels, and unwinds backward as the answer returns.
primers.mechanism:
Watch a tiny function run: factorial(3), which is "3 × 2 × 1". Its rule is: if n is 1, the answer is just 1 (the base case); otherwise the answer is n × factorial(n-1).

Step 1 — Call factorial(3). A crate is placed on the platform stamped [n=3]. It CAN'T finish yet: to return "3 × factorial(2)" it first needs factorial(2). So it freezes, paused on the line `return n * factorial(n-1)`, remembering "I still owe a ×3."

Step 2 — A brand-new crate stacks ON TOP: [n=2]. Note it has its OWN n. It also can't finish; it freezes owing "×2."

Step 3 — Another crate stacks on top: [n=1]. This one hits the base case (`if n == 1: return 1`). It does NOT call another copy — it answers 1 immediately and glows green.

Step 4 — Now the pile shrinks. The [n=1] crate lifts off and hands "1" down. The [n=2] crate un-freezes exactly where it stopped, computes 2 × 1 = 2, lifts off, hands "2" down. The [n=3] crate un-freezes, computes 3 × 2 = 6, lifts off. Platform empty. Final answer: 6.

The whole trick: only the TOP crate is ever awake. Everyone below is frozen mid-sentence. The pile grows as the question goes up, and the real math happens on the way back DOWN as answers pass from crate to crate.
primers.theOneAha: There is no single function "looping." There are many separate frozen copies stacked in a column, each with its own private numbers, and only the one on top is awake. Recursion is just this column growing as questions travel up and shrinking as answers travel back down — and the base case is the ONLY thing that turns the column around. Remove it and the column never stops growing.
primers.trivialHandsOn: No problem to solve — just poke and watch. A single crate labeled count(3) sits on the platform with a big glowing "poke" button. Tap it: a copy count(2) slides up on top, then count(1), then count(0) — and count(0) flashes green and stops (that's the base case). Then watch the column collapse: each crate lifts off, top to bottom, until the platform is empty. Drag the little depth slider to change the starting number and poke again — the column grows to exactly that height. Then flip the "base case" toggle OFF and poke once: watch the crates keep stacking past the top of the screen, faster and faster, until the POWER meter browns out red and the tower topples. You didn't compute anything — you just felt why the base case has to be there.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Beginners assume "a function calling itself" means one function magically looping, with a single n that keeps getting overwritten. The crates show the truth: each call gets its OWN crate with its OWN n — factorial(3)'s n is still 3, sitting frozen at the bottom, while factorial(2)'s n=2 is on the crate above it. They don't share a variable; they stack as separate copies. The second trap: expecting the final answer to appear at the deepest call. The deepest call only produces the SMALL base value (like 1) — the real work happens on the way back down as each crate un-freezes and combines its remembered number with the answer handed up from above. Third: thinking `return` jumps back to the top of the pile; it doesn't — it hands the value to the one crate directly below, which resumes right where it paused.
primers.feedsInto: This unlocks Depth-First Search (DFS) — walking a tree or a maze — which is the first real problem where the call stack you just watched IS the tool doing the work. "Go one step deeper" is a new crate pushed on top; hitting a dead-end or a leaf is the base case; "back up and try another way" is a crate lifting off. Once the growing/shrinking column feels natural, DFS stops looking like magic and looks like the column exploring. The gentlest first bite before that is recursive binary search on the familiar number tape: each guess halves the search and calls a smaller copy of itself, so the vertical stack and the horizontal tape you already know meet in one picture.
primers.clientVisual: Reuse the exact machine-shop crates, but stand them up: the "call stack" is a VERTICAL column of crates rising off the platform, instead of the horizontal number tape. Each crate is one paused copy, stamped with its own arguments (n=3) and a little bookmark showing the code line it's frozen on ("where was I"). Reuse the pointer robot — here a single active-frame robot (call it PC) that always rides the TOP crate, the only one awake; every crate below it is dimmed and frozen. Making a call: a fresh crate slides up onto the top and the robot climbs to it, and the STEPS/ops meter ticks just like today. Returning: the crate glows green (base case) or completes, lifts off, and a value token slides DOWN into the crate below, whose highlighted code line resumes — the code card's active-line highlight now lives on whichever crate the robot is standing on. Repurpose the POWER bar as a DEPTH meter: the taller the column, the more it drains; with the base case toggled off it browns out red and the tower visibly topples — the same brown-out language players already know, now meaning "stack overflow." The scrubber still scrubs: dragging it replays the column growing and shrinking, the highlight hopping between crates. primers.plainDefinition: A tree is a bunch of value-boxes connected by strings. One box sits at the very top, and every other box hangs underneath some box above it. Each box can have up to two strings leading down to two more boxes — the one on the left and the one on the right. That's the whole thing: boxes, and short strings joining a box to the (at most two) boxes hanging below it.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: A baby's crib mobile, or one of those hanging art mobiles. A single box is tied to the ceiling. From its underside, two more little boxes dangle on strings — one to the left, one to the right. From each of those, two more can dangle, and so on. Now imagine you're a tiny climber who can only ever stand on ONE box at a time. You can't teleport and you can't jump sideways to a box across the room — you can only grab a string that hangs off the box you're standing on and slide DOWN it to the box tied at the other end. You always start on the top box, because that's the only one you're handed. Everything else, you reach by sliding down strings.
primers.mechanism:
Step 1 — Meet one box. A tree box holds a value (say the number 8), and it has two hooks on its underside, labelled `.left` and `.right`. A hook is not a direction in space — it's just a named slot, like two labelled coat hooks.

Step 2 — A hook is either tied or empty. `.left` might have a string tied to another box (holding, say, 3). `.right` might have a string to a box holding 10. Or a hook can dangle with nothing tied to it — an empty hook is called `None` (Python's word for "nothing here"). An empty hook is a dead end: there's no string to slide down.

Step 3 — You only ever hold ONE box. The climber robot stands on the top box, the `root` — "root" just means the single box at the top that holds the whole mobile up, the one place you're allowed to start. Its value shows in the read-out: 8.

Step 4 — Moving = following a string. To go to the left child, the robot does `box.left`: it grabs the `.left` string and slides down to the box tied there. The read-out flips to 3. It did NOT walk left across a row — it descended one string. That single move is one hop.

Step 5 — Repeat, and a shape appears. From the box holding 3, the robot can again pick `.left` or `.right` and slide down again. Do this over and over and you're walking a branching path downward. The "tree" is just what you get when you keep repeating one tiny move: stand on a box, pick left or right, slide down.

Step 6 — Where it ends. Some boxes have both hooks empty — nothing hangs below them. Those bottom boxes are called `leaves`. When the robot reaches a leaf, there's no string left to slide down; that branch is finished.

That's every rule. There is no rule 7. A tree is boxes, two named strings per box, and "slide down one string at a time," forever.
primers.theOneAha: A tree is NOT one big scary shape you have to picture all at once. Wherever you're standing, you only ever see one box and exactly two labelled strings — `.left` and `.right` — and your only move is "pick one and slide down." The intimidating branching diagram is just what emerges after you repeat that one tiny local choice a few times. You never actually deal with "the tree." You only ever deal with the box under your feet.
primers.trivialHandsOn: A tiny 3-box mobile is already hung for you: a top box holding 8, with 3 dangling on its `.left` string and 10 on its `.right`. There's nothing to find and no goal. Just poke it: flick the climber robot onto the `.left` string — watch it slide down and the value read-out flip from 8 to 3. Send it back up and flick it down `.right` — it lands on 10. Now, while standing on the box holding 3, try to flick the robot down THAT box's `.left` string, which is empty. The robot just tugs a string that isn't there, stays put, and a little "None" tag wiggles at the dead-end hook. That's it — you're just feeling that `.left` and `.right` move you to two different boxes, and that an empty hook goes nowhere.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: Two things trip up beginners hard. (1) They think `.left` / `.right` mean physical directions — "move leftward in space." They don't; they're just the names of a box's two hooks, "child slot one" and "child slot two." A box's `.left` child could even be drawn to the right on screen — the label is what matters, not the position. (2) Coming straight from the array tape, they expect to jump: on the tape you could hit crate #5 instantly by its number. In a tree there are no numbers to jump to. The ONLY way to reach a box is to start at the top box and follow the strings down to it, one hop at a time. Also worth naming: the tree is drawn root-at-top and grows downward, which feels upside-down compared to a real plant — that's normal, and you always travel DOWN, never up.
primers.feedsInto: Searching a Binary Search Tree (LeetCode 700, "Search in a BST") — the gentlest first real problem, because it gives the left/right choice an actual meaning. In a search tree, every box is arranged so smaller values hang on `.left` and bigger values hang on `.right`. So to find a number you stand on the root, compare, and slide down `.left` if your target is smaller or `.right` if it's bigger — exactly the one move this primer taught, now with a reason to pick a side. From there it opens up to visiting every box (traversal) and measuring how deep the mobile hangs (max depth).

The value-boxes are the same crate art from the array tape — but instead of sitting in a numbered row, they hang in space from strings. The root crate is pinned to a ceiling beam at the top of the canvas. From each crate's underside hang two short labelled strings, `.left` and `.right`; a tied string runs to a child crate, an untied one ends in a frayed tag reading `None`. Use a single pointer robot (the climber, "CUR") — the L/R robots from two-pointer levels aren't two positions here; instead the ONE robot carries a little left/right selector, and choosing a side animates it sliding down that string to the child crate, with the value read-out updating on arrival. Keep the meters, re-labelled for a tree: the `tick` op/step meter counts one per string-slide (a "hop"), so the learner literally watches the counter tick up as they descend; the `space_hi` meter shows how deep the robot currently hangs below the root (this quietly pre-seeds recursion/stack-depth later). The code panel and active-line highlight stay exactly as-is: as the robot slides down `.left`, the line `node = node.left` lights up — same frame/scrubber machinery as the solved levels, so the learner can scrub the descent back and forth.
