Pick one."), and no timer, no pass/fail.

primers.plainDefinition: A graph is just dots connected by lines: the dots are things (cities, people, web pages) and a line means "these two are directly linked." BFS and DFS are two ways to walk from dot to dot until you've seen every dot exactly once — BFS fans out evenly ring by ring, DFS dives down one path as far as it goes before backing up. The "visited" set is a little memory of dots you've already been to, so you never walk in circles forever.
primers.realWorldAnalogy: Picture a museum where rooms are connected by doorways. Two visitors explore it differently. Visitor BFS is like water flooding in from the entrance: it fills every room one doorway away, THEN every room two doorways away — an even, spreading wave. Visitor DFS is a single person who picks a doorway and keeps going straight, room after room, until they hit a dead end, then walks back to the last fork and tries the next door. And crucially, each visitor chalks an X on every room they enter — so when they arrive at a room that already has an X, they turn around instead of wandering the same loop of rooms forever.
primers.mechanism:
Watch it built up in five beats, nothing asserted:

1) The map. Six crates sit on a board, each labelled A–F. Glowing wires connect some pairs — a wire means "these two are neighbors." That's the whole graph: dots plus who-is-linked-to-whom. Nothing moves yet; this is just the terrain.

2) Two pieces of memory. Every crate gets a lamp on its lid, grey = "not visited yet." Off to the side sits a to-do pile (drawn as the familiar numbered tape): the names of dots we've spotted but haven't explored.

3) One rule, looped. Take a name off the to-do pile → the explorer-robot hops along a wire to that crate → flip its lamp green (mark visited) → look down each wire out of it, and for every neighbor whose lamp is still grey, drop that neighbor's name onto the to-do pile. Repeat until the pile is empty. Run this once and you'll notice: this single loop is ALL there is.

4) The one choice that splits BFS from DFS. When you "take a name off the pile," do you grab the OLDEST name waiting or the NEWEST one?
   - Oldest-first = a queue (a first-come-first-served waiting line). You clear everyone one wire from the start, then everyone two wires away — the green lamps light up in expanding rings. This is BFS.
   - Newest-first = a stack (a pile of plates, last one dropped is first grabbed). You immediately chase the neighbor you just discovered, plunging down one path until a crate has no grey neighbors left (a dead end). The pile then hands you back the most recent fork you skipped, so you backtrack and try that. This is DFS.
   Same loop, same map, same visited-marking — only the pickup end changed, and the shape of the exploration flipped completely.

5) Why the lamps exist. Add a loop to the map: A–B–C–A. Switch the lamps OFF (no visited memory) and hit play — the robot walks A→B→C→A→B→C… forever. Switch them back ON and the moment it returns to A, that lamp is already green, so it skips and the walk actually ends. The visited set is the single thing that guarantees you stop.
primers.theOneAha: BFS and DFS are not two algorithms to memorize — they are literally the SAME loop (grab a dot, mark it, drop its unvisited neighbors on a pile, repeat). The only difference is which end of the pile you grab from: oldest-first gives you spreading rings (BFS), newest-first gives you a deep plunge-and-backtrack (DFS). The order you pull your to-do items = the shape of your search. That's it.
primers.trivialHandsOn:
Two no-goal pokes, nothing to solve:
Poke 1 — On a tiny 6-dot map, grab the "grab next from" lever and flip it between OLDEST and NEWEST, then hit play. Same map both times; watch the lamps light up in neat rings one way and in a deep single-file dive the other. Just flip and watch the shape change.
Poke 2 — Find the map's little loop, toggle the "visited memory" switch OFF, and hit play. The robot circles the loop forever and the op-meter climbs without end. Toggle it back ON and watch the run finally stop the instant it hits an already-green lamp. You're not fixing anything — you're just feeling what the visited set is FOR.
primers.commonBeginnerConfusion: The big one: beginners treat BFS and DFS as two separate scary recipes to cram, and they mix up the queue (take oldest) versus the stack (take newest) — when in truth it's one loop with one switch. A second trap is confusing the map with the walk: the graph (the dots and wires) never changes; BFS/DFS are just different ORDERS of visiting the same fixed map. And the classic beginner reflex is "why bother with a visited set — I'd obviously never revisit a dot," which holds right up until the map has a loop and the robot spins in a circle forever. (Bonus mix-up: a tree is just a graph that happens to have no loops, so it needs no visited set — which is why tree traversal felt simpler.)
primers.feedsInto: "Number of Islands" (a.k.a. flood fill): given a grid of land/water cells, count the separate land blobs. It's the gentlest real payoff — each cell is a dot, adjacent cells are wired neighbors, and you just run this exact visit-and-mark loop (BFS or DFS, your pick) with a visited set to sweep each blob once. From there the same machinery unlocks shortest-path-in-a-maze, where BFS's ring-by-ring spread hands you the fewest-steps answer for free.
primers.clientVisual: Reuse the established substrate, lifted off the single line onto a 2D board. Dots = the familiar labelled crates, scattered on the board; edges = glowing wires/rails between crate pairs. The explorer is the same pointer-robot, now hopping along a wire from crate to crate. Each crate gets a lid-lamp: grey = unvisited, green = visited — and the visited set is ALSO mirrored on the classic bottom tape (one slot per dot-id, flipping grey→green) so the learner sees the abstract "set" as concrete crates. The to-do pile is the numbered tape reused as a side loading-dock/conveyor: a "grab next from" lever sits at its two ends — a front-robot (oldest, queue/BFS) and a back-robot (newest, stack/DFS) — and only one is lit per run. BFS colours the green lamps in distance bands (ring 1, ring 2…); DFS trails a glowing string behind the robot that visibly reels back on each backtrack. The op/step meter counts hops and pile-pushes; the scrubber replays the spread frame by frame; and the code panel highlights the active line of the one shared loop, so the learner sees the identical code driving both the rings and the plunge — only the lever differs. A "visited memory" toggle lets Poke 2's infinite loop happen live, with the meter spinning up as the visual proof.

jargonUnexplained: "ops" in the STEPS(ops) meter, and more fundamentally what a "step" even IS and why anyone counts them — the whole payoff hinges on this meter but it's never explained that a step = a unit of work and fewer = faster.

The `nums[3]` / `nums[i]` square-bracket notation (and the name `nums`) — it appears cold in the commonBeginnerConfusion section and the code card, but the tour only ever talks about crates/boxes and never bridges 'the crate at index 3' to the actual syntax `nums[3]`.
"address" (analogy) — used as a plain synonym for the painted number, but 'address' is itself a loaded term the beginner hasn't met; borderline but leans on future jargon.
"N" in 'N identical crates' — mathematical shorthand for 'some count,' unexplained to a non-math reader.
"indices" (in 'valid indices are 0,1,2,3,4') — the plural of index may read as a brand-new word to a beginner who just learned 'index.'
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Mostly yes on the core idea, with a few real snags. The centerpiece is genuinely strong: index = distance from the front, shown (not asserted) via the FRONT marker, the dashed ruler, front + 3 x width computed in one stroke, and the in-between crates never lighting up. That's a well-built aha, and it earns the 'counting starts at 0' and 'box 500 costs the same as box 0' conclusions honestly rather than declaring them. The trivial hands-on (drag, watch +1, thunk into the wall) is exactly right for this learner. BUT three things risk turning the aha into a nod-along. (1) The emotional punchline is 'same cost every time,' yet the primer never tells him what the STEPS meter measures or why he should care — a step is never defined as 'work the machine does' and cost is never tied to speed, so a true beginner may watch the number tick and think 'okay... and?' The walk-vs-jump contrast is shown, which helps, but the significance is left implicit. (2) The metaphor and the code never shake hands: the tour lives entirely in crate-world, then commonBeginnerConfusion and the code card suddenly speak `nums[3]` / `x = nums[i]`. He happens to write Python so list-indexing may feel vaguely familiar, but the primer shouldn't rely on that — it never says 'the square brackets mean look up the box at this index, and nums is just the name of the whole row.' (3) The analogy quietly uses 0-based numbering ('lockers 0 through 6 ... locker #7') BEFORE beat 3 explains why counting starts at 0, so it plants a 'why zero?' question several paragraphs before it's answered — and even mixes notation (#7 with a hash, 0 through 6 without). Net: he'll get the geometry of access, but may miss why it matters and may not connect it to code he'll actually type.
fixes: Define a 'step' the first time the STEPS meter ticks, in one caption: e.g. 'A step is one piece of work the machine does. Fewer steps = faster. Watch — every read costs exactly 1.' Without this the constant-cost aha lands as a curiosity, not the point of the whole tour.

Bridge the crate metaphor to the code notation explicitly, BEFORE the confusion section relies on it. Add a beat/caption mapping `nums[3]` -> 'the crate at index 3,' stating that the square brackets mean 'look up the box at this index number' and that `nums` is just the name of the whole row. Wire the code card `x = nums[i]` to the ruler action: 'i is the index; nums[i] jumps to that crate and hands you the value inside.'

Fix the premature 0-indexing in the analogy. Either postpone 0-based counting to beat 3 where it's explained, or add half a sentence in the analogy ('yes, the first locker is numbered 0 — you'll see exactly why in a moment'). Also make numbering notation consistent (drop the '#7' vs '0 through 6' mismatch).

Standardize on ONE container word. The primer says boxes (definition), lockers (analogy), then crates (mechanism/visual). Pick one after the analogy — likely 'crate,' since that's the actual visual — or add a single line 'the boxes/lockers are drawn as crates in DEREF' so he doesn't wonder whether a crate is a different thing than a box.
Replace 'N identical crates' with a concrete count ('5 identical crates') or 'a handful of crates.' 'N' is unexplained math shorthand for a reader who learns by concrete visuals.
Gloss 'indices' the first time it appears ('index numbers' or '(indices = more than one index)'), so it doesn't read as a new vocabulary word right after he just learned 'index.'

Optional motivational close: one caption tying it forward — 'This jump-straight-to-any-box move is why arrays are the starting point for almost every algorithm' — so the constant-cost fact feels consequential, not trivia, before he moves on to the linear scan.

jargonUnexplained: "position = number × crate-width" (shown on screen per clientVisual): "crate-width" is never explained and is irrelevant to the concept; worse, it overloads the word "position" — earlier "position" means the index (a slot number), here it means a pixel x-coordinate. Two meanings, one word.

"index" / 0-based counting: leaned on throughout ("tape[0]", "crate labeled 0", "biggest index") and grounded via crate labels, but never restated in plain words in-body as "the crate's number, and we start counting at 0." A lost beginner will wonder why the far-left crate is 0 and not 1.

"traversal" and "auto-increments" (in feedsInto teaser): new terms; glossed inline but "traversal" as a label still lands before its plain-English meaning if surfaced on screen. Body wisely says "add one / subtract one" then switches to "auto-increment" here — inconsistent register.
tape[i] bracket notation: the aha rests entirely on the learner already reading nums[i] fluently (declared prereq array-indexing), which the profile says he has NOT internalised.
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Mostly yes — the spine is genuinely strong and well-pitched: the bookmark/finger-under-the-word analogy is concrete, \"poke [+1] and exactly ONE thing changes (L = L + 1)\" is a clean single-variable trace, and the payoff — \"the i in nums[i] WAS a pointer the whole time, moving it is just i = i + 1\" — is the right aha and directly ties to Python he already writes. The two side-by-side tiles (\"L = 2\" vs \"points at tape[2] = 90\") also directly defuse the exact confusion the primer names. But three things risk turning the aha into confused nodding. (1) The on-screen callout \"position = number × crate-width\" injects pixel-layout multiplication that has NOTHING to do with the data-structure idea and re-uses \"position\" to mean something new — a beginner may now think a pointer somehow involves crate-width. (2) The hands-on lesson that spamming [+1] past the last crate \"parks and won't fall off because it's only a number\" is backwards: a number L = L + 1 does NOT self-limit, so this quietly teaches that pointers can't run past valid data — the exact opposite of the #1 beginner bug (off-by-one / IndexError) — and it contradicts the primer's own \"+1 is exactly L = L + 1\" claim. (3) The demo shows L / tape and literal tape[0], but the aha talks about i / nums and tape[L] — the learner has to silently substitute L↔i and tape↔nums himself, which is the one bridge you don't want him to miss. Fix those three and it lands cleanly; leave them and a careful, easily-lost beginner nods along with a slightly wrong model.
fixes: Cut or bury the on-screen "position = number × crate-width" callout. It adds pixel math irrelevant to the concept and overloads "position" (index vs. pixel x). The crate's own "0/1/2/3" label already proves placement — narrate "the robot sits ON crate number L," and keep any `left: index * cw` math as a builder-only code comment, never on the learner's screen.

Fix the clamp-at-the-end behavior. Don't have [+1] "park" at the last crate justified by "it's only a number so it won't fall off" — that reasoning is backwards and contradicts "+1 is exactly L = L + 1." Instead let L reach 4 and show the POINTS-AT tile go empty ("nothing here — past the end"), planting the true idea: a pointer is just a number that CAN point past the data, and that's where IndexError comes from. At minimum, delete the "won't fall off because it's just a number" line.

Bridge L↔i and tape↔nums explicitly at the aha moment. The demo uses L/tape; the aha talks i/nums. Add one on-screen line right at the reveal: "L is just your Python i — and tape[L] is just nums[i]." Don't make the beginner perform the substitution in his head.

Show tape[L] instead of the literal tape[0] in the POINTS-AT tile (e.g. "POINTS AT tape[L] = 90" beside the "L = 2" tile). Putting the pointer variable inside the brackets on screen makes the core aha — the pointer IS the thing that goes in [ ] — visible, while the separate "L = 2" tile still isolates position (2) from content (90). Keep both tiles so the position-vs-content split stays crisp.

Add a single in-context line that counting starts at 0 ("the first crate is number 0, not 1") the first time the robot sits at the far left, so a lost beginner isn't quietly tripped by 0-based indexing.

Keep the plain "add one / subtract one" phrasing everywhere learner-facing; if the feedsInto teaser is shown, replace "auto-increments" / "traversal" with "a normal for-loop is secretly one pointer walking right by itself, adding one each pass."

jargonUnexplained: "Big-O" itself: the primer teaches the FEELING of growth beautifully but never once shows the actual symbol (O(n), O(n²)). A concept literally named "bigo" that never connects the felt gap to the notation the learner will meet in every interview/doc/tutorial leaves them able to feel it but unable to NAME it. He'll watch this, get the aha, then see "O(n²)" elsewhere and not realize it's the same thing he just held in his hands.

"comparing" (SLOW lane): the robot R "compares L's crate against each other crate" — but this is billed as a pure no-problem tour, so a beginner immediately asks "comparing to find WHAT?" and there's no answer given. The word smuggles in a hidden task and can stall him on a question the tour deliberately refuses to answer yet.

"work" (in the definition): the opening sentence hangs the whole idea on "amount of work," but "work" isn't grounded until the op-meter is defined several beats later. On first read "work" is abstract — a beginner can't tell if it means keystrokes, seconds, memory, or lines of code.
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Mostly yes, and better than most Big-O explanations he's seen — but with a few real snags. The roll-call-vs-handshakes analogy is genuinely intuitive, the two-meters-plus-slider hands-on is exactly the see-it-not-solve-it experience this learner asked for, and theOneAha (rubber band vs explosion) is crisply isolated so the takeaway is unmistakable. He would very likely FEEL the gap yawn open on the slider and walk away with the correct core intuition. The snags: (1) the same two things get THREE different names — roll call/handshakes, FAST/SLOW, rubber-band/explosion — and the primer never explicitly maps them onto each other, so an easily-lost beginner has to silently guess these are all the same pair. (2) Naming the lanes \"FAST/SLOW\" actively fights the lesson \"it's not a stopwatch,\" because fast/slow ARE time words; the commonBeginnerConfusion section rescues this, but only later. (3) He gets the sensation but is never handed the vocabulary token (O(n)/O(n²)) that the rest of the world uses, so the intuition is stranded from the symbol. Net: he gets the aha, not just a confused nod — provided the two prereq tours (crates, pointer-robots) were actually played first, since this primer leans on that vocabulary without re-teaching it.
fixes: Unify the naming with ONE visible mapping. Pick a single label pair (the growth words "gentle-grow / steep-grow" are safest) and show once, on screen, that roll call = gentle = rubber-band = O(n) and handshakes = steep = explosion = O(n²). Three metaphors for two ideas is too many pegs for an easily-lost beginner unless you nail them together explicitly.

Defuse the FAST/SLOW-vs-seconds tension at the moment the labels appear, not two sections later. Either rename the lanes to growth words, or park the "when n is tiny, the SLOW one is often just as quick — sometimes quicker" caveat right next to the labels so he's never briefly misled into thinking slow = always worse = seconds.

Give the SLOW robot's 'comparing' a reason or strip the word. In a no-problem tour, say "R just visits every other crate — never mind why yet, we're only counting touches," and optionally foreshadow one line: "later this becomes hunting for a matching pair (that's Two Sum)." Right now 'comparing' implies a task the tour refuses to explain, which stalls the learner.

Attach the intuition to the symbol at the very end. After the aha, add one calm beat: "the gentle one is written O(n); the explosive one O(n²) — that's literally all those symbols mean." Without this the learner feels Big-O but can't recognize it when he sees the notation everywhere else.

Make the numbers tell ONE consistent story. The handshake analogy uses unique pairs (~435 for 30 people) while the crate meter uses whole-tape re-sweeps (~100 for 10 crates = n²), and clientVisual says 'once per pair' — three slightly different counting rules. Either align them or add a one-liner: "the exact totals differ, but both quadruple when you double the pile — the growth is the whole point."

Ground "work" in the very first definition. Add half a sentence: "'work' here means one robot touching one crate — the thing the op meter counts," so the abstract opening has a concrete anchor before the mechanism arrives.

Micro-explain the growth graph and soften the 'zero new visual vocabulary' claim. A two-axis plotted curve IS new relative to crates/robots/meters. Label the axes in plain words ("crates on the tape" → across, "clicks on the meter" → up), never "n" and "operations," and add one line: "this graph just re-draws the meter reading as you drag the slider."

Introduce "n = how many crates" the first time the tape grows (in the mechanism), not for the first time in the hands-on section, since commonBeginnerConfusion leans on n heavily and the earlier grow-the-tape reveal already needs it.

jargonUnexplained: "binary search" and "two-pointer" — dropped inside the MECHANISM ("Binary search and two-pointer are nothing more than clever ways of always standing where...") before they're ever taught. Reading that, a lost beginner thinks "I'm supposed to already recognise these" and feels behind. They belong in feedsInto (where they're fine); the flaw is naming them mid-explanation as if known.

"op meter" / "op" — the abbreviation "op" (operation) is never spelled out. It's semi-self-explaining ("clicks up... for every crate it inspects"), but it also clashes with the on-screen tally the clientVisual calls "crates checked" — so the narration and the actual UI label use two different words for the exact same thing, which beginners anchor hard on.

"the atom" ("one comparison erasing a whole region — is the atom") — used metaphorically to mean "the fundamental unit," but a beginner reads the literal science word and stalls. Needs a four-word gloss.

"tape" / "crates" / "pointer-robot" — the entire explanation rides on this metaphor but it is never re-stated inside this doc; it relies wholly on the prereq levels having been done and remembered. No one-line reminder is given.
"≤" / "≥" — a Python dev knows the symbols, but for someone described as "genuinely easily lost" they should be said in words the first time ("≤ 4, i.e. 4 or smaller").
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Mostly YES — and that's the honest headline. The dictionary analogy (flip to 'M', toss the first half you never read, then the shuffled-dictionary counter-example) is genuinely excellent and lands the intuition before any abstraction. The 'watch the same tape twice' mechanism (shuffled [4,9,1,7,3,8] vs sorted [1,3,4,7,8,9], same poke, wildly different amount going dark) shows rather than asserts. And the commonBeginnerConfusion ('how can you be SURE 7 isn't on the left if the robot never looked?') is precisely the question a real beginner asks, answered by a rule instead of a hunch. So he'd get the real aha, not just nod along. BUT there is one spot that risks turning the aha into a stall, and it's the interactive step — the part he actually touches. The trivialHandsOn insists 'No target, no goal, nothing to find,' yet it then shows a curtain over 'the whole region that just became impossible' and a counter that ticks 'ruled out without looking.' Impossible for WHAT? Ruled out relative to WHAT? With no target there's no referent, so the payoff of the demo undercuts its own framing. Worse, the clientVisual quietly contradicts the hands-on: it DOES have a 'target readout,' fires a beam that resolves to '4 < 7,' and labels the curtain '≤ 4 — skip' — all of which presuppose the target the hands-on says doesn't exist. A careful beginner poking around will feel the seam. Add the mid-stream name-drop of binary search/two-pointer and the metaphor being assumed rather than restated, and the verdict is: strong primer that will teach the insight, with two or three local snags that could make him feel briefly lost in exactly the interactive moment meant to cement it.
fixes: Resolve the target contradiction (biggest issue). trivialHandsOn says 'No target, no goal, nothing to find,' but clientVisual has a 'target readout,' a '4 < 7' verdict beam, and a '≤ 4 — skip' label, and the counter is literally 'ruled out without looking.' Ruling-out only means something against a target. Pick ONE frame: either give the hands-on a soft target (a faint 'looking for 7' chip) so 'ruled out' has a referent, OR relabel the sorted curtain as 'now KNOWN without looking — all ≤ 4' (not 'ruled out / became impossible / skip') so it works with genuinely no goal. As written, the two sections fight each other.

Make the demo numbers actually add up. Sorted is [1,3,4,7,8,9]; poking the crate showing 4 leaves only {1,3} to its left, so the honest count is 'ruled out: 2', not the '3' the copy shows. With the scrubber available, a beginner WILL replay and count. Either change the copy to 2, or have the robot poke the crate showing 7 (then {1,3,4} = 3 is correct).

Stop naming binary search and two-pointer inside the mechanism. Rewrite the closing line as 'the fast searches you'll meet next are nothing more than clever ways of always standing where this erase-a-region move pays off the most' and let feedsInto introduce the names. Don't reference concepts he hasn't met while he's mid-aha.

Gloss the jargon on first use and unify labels with the UI: 'op meter' → 'checks counter — each tick is one crate the robot actually looked at,' and use that same phrase as the on-screen tally (clientVisual currently says 'crates checked' — make narration and UI identical). 'the atom' → 'the atom: the one smallest move everything else is built from.'

Add a one-line metaphor reminder at the top of plainDefinition or mechanism so the doc stands alone even if a prereq was skipped or forgotten: '(the tape is our array; each crate holds one number; the robot is a pointer that can sit on exactly one crate at a time).' Say ≤/≥ in words the first time they appear.

Unify the 'no promise' wording, which currently appears three ways: mechanism 'order gives no promise,' handsOn caption 'the others could be anything,' clientVisual 'no promise about the neighbours.' Beginners memorise exact labels — pick one phrase and use it in all three places.

jargonUnexplained: "hash" / "hashing" — the concept's own name, baked into hash map / hash set / hash gadget, is used purely as a label and never defined; the learner never finds out that "to hash" means "run a value through the rule to get its slot number."
"address" — appears only in theOneAha ("computes its own address"); the entire mechanism says "slot"/"hole," so "address" reads like a newly introduced term rather than a synonym.
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: He'll get the CORE aha and it'll land: value computes its own slot, so you jump instead of scan, and you paid for it with the wall of space — that's shown well via the STEPS-vs-AUX-SPACE contrast and the deliberate teleport-not-walk visual. The primer also handles its listed prereqs honestly, re-defining n, O(n), and O(1) inline so a shaky beginner isn't stranded. BUT he'll snag hard on one thing: the wall is fixed at ten holes (0-9) the whole time, yet he's told 'a million values still costs 1 step' and 'collisions are rare.' A skeptic looking at ten holes will think 'a million values into ten holes would pile up — that can't be one step, and collisions can't be rare.' He's right: those two claims are only true because real hash maps keep MORE holes than items and grow the wall with the data — a fact the primer never states. So it quietly leans on an unstated 'the wall grows' assumption (knowledge he doesn't have) to make its headline claims true, and its collision reassurance is asserted rather than shown (a list-inside-a-hole is exactly the slow tape-walk he was just warned off). Net: he gets the beautiful part and then hits a wall — literally — on scale and collisions, and either carries a wrong mental model or feels hand-waved.
fixes: FIX THE CONTRADICTION (highest priority): state explicitly that the wall is kept BIGGER than the pile and GROWS as you add values — roughly one-plus holes per item. This single sentence is what makes both headline claims honest: it's why AUX SPACE balloons AND why a lookup stays 1 step even at a million values. Right now a permanently 10-hole wall plus 'a million values still 1 step' is a flat contradiction he can see on screen.

GROUND 'collisions are rare' IN THAT SAME MECHANISM instead of asserting it. Show it: a hole only holds more than one crate when two values hash to the same slot; because the wall is kept roomier than the pile, that's uncommon — and be honest that when it does happen, that hole becomes a tiny tape you walk, so the bad case degrades back toward the slow scan. Don't just tell him 'rare'; his 10-hole toy makes crowding look common, so you must show why it isn't.

DEFINE 'hash' once, plainly: 'that rule is called a hash function; to hash a value just means run it through the rule to get its slot number.' Otherwise hash map / hash set / hash gadget stay opaque labels he can't unpack.

PICK STORE EXAMPLES WHERE VALUE != SLOT. Drop 8->hole 8 and other single-digit values (value equals its own slot, which blurs 'value 15' vs 'hole 5 = an address'). Use 15->5, 23->3, 47->7, 90->0, and have the visual clearly label hole numbers as ADDRESSES distinct from crate values.

SHOW dict, don't just claim it. The definition promises dict AND set but the mechanism only does set. Add one beat: a set just remembers 'seen it'; a dict also parks a note in the slot (name -> phone number). This de-risks feedsInto too, since Two Sum actually needs a dict (value -> its index), not a set.
KEEP VOCAB CONSISTENT: the mechanism says 'slot'/'hole' but the aha switches to 'address.' Say 'its slot number (its address)' once, then stick to one word so 'address' doesn't read as a new concept.

Optional polish: the coat-check 'ticket number derived from your coat' is hand-wavy (how do you derive a number from a coat?). Point it straight at the concrete gadget — 'like reading the last digit off your coat-check ticket' — so the analogy and the mechanism reinforce instead of drift.

jargonUnexplained: "array" — appears in the concept title and the confusion section but is never glossed in-primer; it's also silently swapped in for "list"/"tape"/"board", so the beginner can't tell they're the same object
"target" — used from the mechanism onward and in trivialHandsOn ("no target, no goal") but only ever implied via the analogy, never plainly defined as "the number you're aiming for"
"converged" — mechanism says "the robots have converged on the pair"; a beginner may not know the word (say "met")
"single left-to-right sweep" — in theOneAha; not only unexplained but inaccurate (the markers close in from both ends)

O(n) / O(n²) / "brute-force" / "one pass" / "linear" — used in feedsInto; design-facing here, but this vocabulary must not leak into the Tour narration and must be glossed when it first appears in the later problem level
"28 pairs" — the check-everything baseline number is dropped without saying where it comes from (8 crates paired with every other = 28)
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Mostly yes — this is a strong primer and he'd likely get a real aha rather than just nodding, but only if a few concrete flaws are fixed first. The gym-weights analogy is genuinely intuitive and the commonBeginnerConfusion section is the best part: it pre-empts the two classic traps (the pointer 'carries' the number, and you 'choose/guess' which pointer) exactly as a beginner would hit them, and it hammers the make-or-break caveat that this only works because the tape is sorted. The theOneAha ('one comparison wipes out a whole column of pairs') is correct and well-argued. What would tip him from 'aha' into 'nod along confused': (1) the STEPS meter reads 2 in the mechanism while he's told to count '3 looks' — he'll distrust the counter or think he lost the thread; (2) the free-play hands-on is described as coming 'before any rule is stated' yet is ordered AFTER the rules, so the whole point of feeling the squeeze in his hand first is lost; (3) list/array/tape/board used interchangeably for one thing; (4) the definition explains HOW to step markers before ever saying WHAT he's trying to find. Fix those and he gets it; ship as-is and he'll follow the analogy but stumble on the mechanism.
fixes: Resolve the STEPS-count contradiction: mechanism ends at STEPS=2 (counting retires/moves), but the '3 looks' claim and clientVisual ('ticks 1, 2, 3') count comparisons. Make all three agree. Recommended: count LOOKS — tick STEPS on the very first comparison so it reads 1,2,3 and cleanly contrasts with '28 pairs'.

Present the trivialHandsOn free-play BEFORE the narrated mechanism/aha, matching the primer's own line 'before any rule is ever stated.' Reorder the Tour so he feels 'the sum only goes one way' in his hand first, then the rules name what he already felt.

Unify vocabulary: the same object is called list / array / board / tape. Pick one (tape) and gloss the synonyms exactly once ('a list of numbers — we draw it as a tape of crates'). In particular, reconcile 'array' in commonBeginnerConfusion with 'tape' used everywhere else.

State the goal up front in plainDefinition, before the mechanism: add a clause like 'Say you want two numbers that add up to a target number' so the marker-stepping has a purpose from the first sentence.
Fix theOneAha wording: replace 'a single left-to-right sweep' with 'one pass where the two markers close in from both ends' — the current phrasing contradicts the converging-robots visual.

Reword the muddy line in trivialHandsOn: 'moving a marker inward always changes the sum in one predictable direction' is wrong globally (inward lowers the sum for R, raises it for L). Make it per-marker: 'each marker changes the sum one way and only that way — R always lowers it, L always raises it.'
Gloss 'converged' (mechanism) as plain 'met on the pair,' and add a one-line aside explaining where '28 pairs' comes from.

Keep O(n)/O(n²)/brute-force/POWER-brownout out of the Tour entirely (they live only in feedsInto's later problem level per clientVisual) and gloss them on first appearance there — the beginner has no big-O yet.
Show the clientVisual caption 'the glow means bigger — this tape is sorted small-to-big' BEFORE the walkthrough starts, so 'sorted' is grounded as meaning before any rule leans on it.

jargonUnexplained: O(n) and O(n^2): dropped naked in commonBeginnerConfusion and feedsInto, never defined, not in prereqs. Biggest glaze-over moment for a true beginner, and painful because the STEPS-vs-RECOMPUTE meters already teach this idea visually before the text throws it away in symbols.
'invariant' (step 5): explained inline right after, but the word itself is never defined and is intimidating to lead with.
'ops' (in 'STEPS (ops) meter'): never spelled out as 'operations'; the whole lesson hinges on ops=work.
'index 0' (step 1): assumes array-indexing vocabulary; a Python user likely survives it but it is used before it is grounded.
'substring' (feedsInto): appears with no gloss, lower-stakes as a forward pointer.
'running number/value' (plainDefinition): 'running' meaning kept-up-to-date is colloquial and never unpacked.
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Mostly yes on the core aha, with a few real stumbles. The mechanism section is the star: it changes numbers one beat at a time, flashes the entering crate green (+) and the leaving crate red (-), and the STEPS-vs-RECOMPUTE ghost meter RENDERS the 'why bother' payoff instead of asserting it. That is exactly the mechanism-first, show-don't-tell teaching he needs, and the 'no goal, just poke the edges and watch the number breathe' hands-on directly answers his complaint that concepts get thrown at him as problems. He would genuinely feel the aha: the total only changes by what crosses an edge. BUT three spots flip him from getting-it to nodding-along-confused. (1) The abstract Big-O sentences: right after being taught visually, he hits O(n) and O(n^2) with zero definition, a hard stop that undercuts the visual win. (2) The analogy sells a FIXED frame that slides (one coin out AND one in, together), but the mechanism and the two buttons decompose motion into separate GROW (only add) and SHRINK (only subtract) moves, so he wonders 'why two buttons when the coins moved as one?' The confusion trap names this but the flow never bridges it. (3) Both buttons read 'step R ->' and 'step L ->' with arrows pointing right, yet moving L rightward makes the window SMALLER, which is easy to misread as 'everything just moves right.' A nagging inconsistency too: the mechanism starts the window 1 crate wide (both robots on crate 0) while the hands-on starts it 3 wide (crates 0-2), so the numbers he is told to expect will not line up with the walk-through he just read.
fixes: Kill the naked Big-O or ground it. Replace O(n)/O(n^2) with the meter language he already saw (STEPS rises by 1 per move; the ghost meter bends upward as the frame widens; the growing gap is the point), OR add one plain sentence defining n = number of crates and tying each notation to one of the two meters. Never leave the symbols undefined.

Bridge the analogy to the mechanism. Add a line: 'A full slide like the coins (one out AND one in) is just a SHRINK plus a GROW; here we split them into two buttons so you can watch each edge on its own.' This kills the why-two-buttons whiplash.

Fix the counterintuitive both-step-right. Label buttons by EFFECT: 'step R -> (grow/add)' and 'step L -> (shrink/drop)', and add a clause in step 4: 'L moving right makes the frame NARROWER because the left edge catches up to the right edge.'

Make the starting width consistent. The analogy uses 3 coins, the mechanism starts 1 crate wide, the hands-on starts 3 wide. Pick one width across all three so the SUM numbers reconcile with the walk-through.

State what the frame COVERS before it moves. Move 'window = crates L to R inclusive, width = R-L+1' up to step 1 (both robots on crate 0) instead of revealing it only at step 5; he needs the frame's meaning, and the off-by-one/inclusive trap, before he watches it change.
Define 'invariant' and 'ops' on first use: 'the one fact that is ALWAYS true no matter where the window sits' and 'STEPS (ops = operations, units of work).'
Gloss 'running number' once: 'you keep ONE number that you keep up to date (a running total) instead of recomputing it.'

jargonUnexplained: 'queue' — named in commonBeginnerConfusion as 'a completely different structure' but never given even a one-line what-it-is; the everyday 'line of people' meaning carries it, yet calling it a *structure* dangles a forward reference a beginner can't cash

append() as the Python name for PUSH — pop() maps to POP by sound, but PUSH and append() share no letters and the prose never states 'PUSH is append()'; the link lives only in the code-card visual, so a reader following the text alone can miss it
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Yes — he'd genuinely get the aha, not just nod along. This is unusually well-scaffolded for exactly his learning style: it leads with a concrete physical thing (the plate tube), runs a step-by-step mechanism trace before asserting anything, and defines every term at the moment it's introduced (LIFO is spelled out the sentence it appears; 'first-in-first-out' is written out too). Critically, it preempts THE trap he'd fall into — expecting 3,7,9 back in order — and names it explicitly. The hands-on ('try to grab the bottom crate, the claw refuses with a shake') turns the one-end rule into something felt, which is precisely mechanism+visual over memorization. The reframe that 'the restriction IS the feature' tied to Undo and the Back button gives him a real hook. The gaps are refinements, not blockers: (1) the PUSH->append() naming bridge is never stated in words, only shown in the code card, so text-only he might not connect the narrated 'PUSH' to the Python he already knows; (2) the Undo/Back-button/bracket claims in theOneAha are asserted, not shown, which slightly violates the product's own 'show, don't assert' rule — though feedsInto later demonstrates the bracket case. None of this assumes DSA knowledge he lacks: the only assumed prior knowledge is Python append/pop/indexing, which is a legitimately listed prereq (python-list-basics) and squarely in his comfort zone. Net: he reaches the real aha, with two small snags that are easy to close.
fixes: State the PUSH<->Python mapping in the PROSE, not just the code card. Add one line to the mechanism section: 'In Python these two moves are literally list.append(x) (that's PUSH) and list.pop() with no argument (that's POP — no index means it takes from the end).' PUSH and append() share no letters, so a text-following reader can miss the connection the visual makes.

Anchor the abstract tube to a Python list EARLY, not only in the confusion trap. Right after the plainDefinition, add: 'A stack isn't a new Python type you have to learn — it's an ordinary list you promise to only ever touch at the end.' This gives the Python-comfortable learner a concrete peg before the abstract mechanism, instead of making him wait until commonBeginnerConfusion to learn it was 'just a list' all along.

Make theOneAha SHOW at least one of its claims instead of asserting three. The product's rule is show-don't-assert, but Undo/Back/brackets are all stated. Add a 2-second micro-trace: relabel the tube's crates as actions — 'type A, type B, Undo' — and show B (the newest) is what disappears first. One demonstrated example beats three asserted ones.

Prove the reversal side-by-side in the hands-on. After pushing 3,7,9 and popping to 9,7,3, flash an explicit 'IN: 3 7 9  ->  OUT: 9 7 3' line on screen. Popping one crate at a time shows newest-first per step, but the beginner's whole misconception is about the OVERALL order — seeing the full sequence reversed at once makes the point undeniable.

Fix the dangling 'queue' reference. Either drop the word entirely — 'a line of people leaves in the order they arrived; a stack does the exact opposite' — or add half a sentence: '(that arrive-order behaviour is its own structure, a queue, which you'll meet later).' As written it names a structure it never explains.

Unpack 'zero bookkeeping' in theOneAha — it's abstract for a beginner. Replace with the concrete payoff: 'you never have to track which item is newest or remember what order things came in — the top is always the newest, automatically.' Say what work you're being spared, not just that you're spared it.

jargonUnexplained: "log time" — the felt intuition is given ("double the haystack, pay one more guess"), but the word "log" is dropped as if the reader already connects it to logarithms/Big-O. A true beginner won't link this to the "O(log n)" he'll meet the moment he opens LeetCode 704.

"the two-pointer view" — the clientVisual and mechanism reuse the L/R robots "from the two-pointer view," assuming he's already played a prior two-pointer tour. Played standalone, this is a dangling reference to a concept never introduced here.

"sorted" — used as THE load-bearing precondition (the whole confusion section hinges on it), yet never defined in one plain line. It's a common word, but given how much weight it carries, a beginner shouldn't have to infer that "sorted" means each crate is >= the one before it.

"(L+R)//2" / midpoint — the formula is shown but never called out as recomputing on the *shrinking window*, not the fixed tape. A beginner can easily miss that the middle moves relative to L and R each step.
critique.wouldATrueBeginnerGetIt: Yes, mostly — this is genuinely strong mechanism-first teaching and he'd very likely get the real aha, not just nod along. The guess-my-number analogy, the crate-by-crate window collapse, and especially the ×2 hands-on (tape floods to a million while the \"guesses needed\" counter lazily ticks 5,6,7...20) are exactly the show-don't-assert, felt-not-memorised style he needs. The core insight (\"a guess kills HALF, not one\") lands hard. BUT there are honest snags that would trip the easily-lost version of him. The worst is a factual mismatch: the mechanism narrates real windows of 16 -> 8 (crates 8..15) -> 3 (crates 8..10) -> 1, but the recap line says \"16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1.\" A beginner watching the animation shrink from 8 crates to 3 crates and then reading \"-> 4 ->\" will feel something is broken — and it silently hides a real question he'll have (odd-sized windows don't split into equal halves). Second, \"log time\" is introduced with good intuition but never named as the thing he'll see written as O(log n), so the bridge from this tour to the actual problem vocabulary is missing. Third, \"sorted\" is the entire safety rule yet never crisply defined. None of these break the core understanding, but for a learner who is \"easily lost\" they're exactly the kind of small cracks that turn confidence into quiet confusion.
fixes: Fix the recap inconsistency: the walkthrough shows windows of 16 -> 8 -> 3 -> 1 crates, but the summary says "16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1." Either match the actual run, or explicitly separate the two ideas: "in this run the window went 16 -> 8 -> 3 -> 1; on a perfectly-halvable pile it'd be 16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1 — the point is it shrinks by ~half each look."

Address odd windows head-on (it's a real beginner 'huh?'): add one narration line like "8 crates can't split perfectly in two, so the middle rounds down and one side gets the extra crate — that's all // does here." He knows Python //, so tie the rounding to something he already owns.

Bridge "log time" to the problem vocabulary: after the felt explanation, add one line — "When you see this written as O(log n) in the problems, THIS is what it means: n explodes, the work barely moves." Otherwise the tour and LeetCode speak different languages.

Define "sorted" in one plain line the first time it's used, since the whole 'permission slip' idea depends on it: "sorted = every crate holds a bigger value than the one before it, smallest on the left to biggest on the right." Then the amber-glow rule has something concrete to point at.

Call out that the MIDDLE moves: add a beat noting the mid is the middle of the *current lit window* (L..R), not the middle of the whole tape — e.g. "notice MID re-centres between the L and R robots each step, not on the original tape." Right now step 2's (8+15)//2 quietly assumes he noticed the middle relocated.

Make the L/R robots self-contained: don't rely on "from the two-pointer view." One clause — "the L and R robots just mark the left and right edges of the crates still in play" — so the tour stands alone if it's his first one.

Optional polish: in step 1, spell out why the discarded half includes the middle crate ("45 wasn't it and everything at/left of it is too small, so 0 through 7 all go dark") — it reinforces why L jumps to 8 and not 7, which is a classic off-by-one confusion.

jargonUnexplained: "leaf" (in feedsInto: "hitting a dead-end or a leaf is the base case") — tree terminology dropped with zero explanation; a beginner has no picture for it.
"frame" / "active-frame" (clientVisual: "a single active-frame robot") — stack-frame jargon used raw; nowhere is it said that a frame = one crate = one paused copy.

# DEREF Basics-First Track — Learning Design Plan

## 0. One structural gap I'm fixing before anything else

Three primers (`fast-vs-slow-bigo`, `why-sorting-helps`, `hashing-o1-lookup`) list a "linear scan / traversal" as a prerequisite, and both `arrays-and-indices` and `pointers-cursors` name the linear scan as their `feedsInto` "first real problem" — but **no primer actually teaches it**. That's a hole a true beginner would fall through. I'm adding one short bridge tour, **`walking-the-tape`** (the linear scan), between pointers and Big-O. It teaches nothing new structurally: one robot walks every crate once, and the STEPS meter counts to N. Its real job is to give the words **step / op / work / N** a concrete, felt anchor *before* Big-O leans on them — which is exactly the fix the Big-O critic demanded ("ground 'work' in the first definition"). It costs almost no new art (single robot, existing tape, existing STEPS meter).

---

## 1. The ordered curriculum

The spine goes: **what a container IS → how we read it → how we measure the cost of reading → how *order* makes reading cheap → how a *different* container makes reading cheap → containers with special rules → linked structures.** Each tour only uses vocabulary a prior tour has already grounded.

**Block A — The array, and how to read one value**
1. **`arrays-and-indices`** — the tape of crates; index = distance from the front. (Root. Its only prereqs, "a value / a variable," are pre-DSA; the learner already writes Python, so I fold a 20-second grounding into the opening rather than making a tour of it.)
2. **`pointers-cursors`** — the robot is just a stored number (`i`); "moving" it is `i = i + 1`.
3. **`walking-the-tape` (NEW)** — one robot visits every crate once; STEPS counts to N. Grounds *step / work / N*.

**Block B — How we talk about cost**
4. **`fast-vs-slow-bigo`** — same tape, two lanes; watch the op meters pull apart as N grows. (Needs the tape + the walk from Block A.)

**Block C — Order is information (the sorted-array line)**
5. **`why-sorting-helps`** — on a sorted tape, one look tells you about a whole region. (Needs tape, the scan, and a plain definition of "sorted," which this tour also supplies for everything downstream.)
6. **`two-pointers`** — the squeeze from both ends. *Built first in the app, so it introduces the L/R robots the next two tours reuse.* (Needs sorted + index-vs-value.)
7. **`binary-search`** — one look kills half the *remaining* window. Reuses L/R (now "the window still in play") and adds MID. (Needs sorted + Big-O for "log time.")
8. **`sliding-window`** — two markers moving the *same* direction; a running total you only fix at the edges. (Needs two-pointers; deliberately *not* sorted.)

**Block D — A different container: pay space to skip the search**
9. **`hashing-o1-lookup`** — the value computes its own slot, so you jump instead of scan; you bought that with memory. Natural contrast to Block C: sorting buys cheap search with *arrangement*; hashing buys it with *space*. (Needs the scan + Big-O.)

**Block E — Containers with a rule about ends, and self-reference**
10. **`stack-lifo`** — touch one end only; last-in-first-out. (Needs arrays + Python list.)
11. **`recursion-callstack`** — a column of frozen copies; the base case turns the column around. (Needs the stack.)

**Block F — Linked structures**
12. **`trees`** — boxes joined by named strings (`.left`/`.right`); you can't jump, you must follow links. Best appreciated *after* Block A made jumping feel free. (Needs pointers + None; I substitute the pointer tour for the missing "linked-lists" prereq — see fix.)
13. **`graphs-bfs-dfs`** — dots and lines; one loop, one switch (oldest vs newest) = BFS vs DFS; a visited set stops the circling. (Needs hashing's set, the stack/queue idea, and builds on trees + recursion.)

After tour 13 the learner is ready for the first *problem* level (Two Sum, Contains Duplicate, Valid Parentheses, Number of Islands, etc.) — each of which is the `feedsInto` of a tour they've already played by hand.

---

## 2. Per-primer fixes, folded in

Every one of the 12 was flagged (assumes prior knowledge and/or unexplained jargon). Concrete decisions:

**1. arrays-and-indices** — (a) Define "step" the first time STEPS ticks: *"A step is one piece of work the machine does. Fewer steps = faster."* (b) Add a beat bridging metaphor→code *before* the confusion section: `nums[3]` = "the crate at index 3"; square brackets = "look up the box at this index"; `nums` = the name of the whole row; wire the `x = nums[i]` card to the ruler action. (c) Fix the premature 0-indexing in the analogy — add *"yes, the first locker is numbered 0 — you'll see why in a moment,"* and drop the `#7`-vs-`0 through 6` notation mismatch. (d) Standardize on **crate** after the analogy (say once "the boxes/lockers are drawn as crates"). (e) Replace "N identical crates" with "**5** identical crates." (f) Gloss "indices" on first use. (g) Add the motivational close: *"jump-straight-to-any-box is why arrays start almost every algorithm."*

(b) **Fix the clamp bug**: don't "park and won't fall off." Let L step past the last crate and show the POINTS-AT tile go empty — *"nothing here — past the end"* — planting the truth that a pointer is a number that *can* point past the data (that's where IndexError comes from). (c) At the aha, put one line on screen: *"L is just your Python `i` — and `tape[L]` is just `nums[i]`."* (d) Show `tape[L]` (not literal `tape[0]`) in the POINTS-AT tile. ## 3. Spec: the DEREF "Guided Tour" mode

**Core promise:** a gentle, narrated, **no-fail** experience with *no problem to solve*. The learner pokes, and the substrate reacts. Every claim in narration must have a **visible cause on screen** at the moment it's made — the tour never asserts what it doesn't show.

### Reused substrate (no new engine)
The tape/crates (`_TapePainter`), the L/R pointer-robots, the scrubber + frame counter, the meter row, and the `_codeCard` with active-line highlight are all reused verbatim. A Guided Tour is a *configuration* of the existing player, not a new player.

### What a tour is made of
Every tour is a fixed sequence of **beats** plus one **free-play sandbox**, in this arc:
1. **Meet the substrate** — the board appears, nothing moving; narration names what's on screen in one line.
2. **One move, step by step** — a single operation animated one beat at a time; each number that changes is shown changing (green "+" / red "−" chips, meter ticks).
3. **The Aha, isolated** — one beat that states the single takeaway, with the on-screen element that proves it highlighted.
4. **Free-play sandbox** — "no goal, nothing to solve, just poke it": steppers / toggles / sliders / draggable robots. Every input is safe (out-of-bounds "thunks," toggles flip, nothing can be wrong).
5. **The common confusion, named** — the one trap this concept springs, shown as a contrast on the same board.
6. **Handoff teaser** — one card naming the first real problem this unlocks.

For the tours that discovered an ordering bug in review (two-pointers), the arc puts **free-play before the narrated mechanism** — feel it in your hand first, then name what you felt.

### Rules the mode enforces (these encode the critiques)
- **Jargon gate:** the first appearance of any term gets an inline gloss chip or one-line caption. A term cannot be shown on screen before it's glossed once.
- **One word per object:** crate / tape / robot — never silently swapped for box / list / array / cursor. Synonyms are introduced once ("a list of numbers — we draw it as a tape of crates") then dropped.
- **Meters tell the truth and nothing else:** only the meters a tour actually uses are lit; the rest are grayed out. (STEPS lit for arrays; SUM for two-pointers; AUX SPACE for hashing; DEPTH for recursion.) An unused meter is never left ticking, because a beginner will try to interpret it.
- **No graded chrome:** no POWER brownout, no TARGET/SOLVED verdict chips, no timer, no Run button, no pass/fail. Those belong only to problem levels.
- **Autoplay off:** beats advance on tap or scrub; the learner controls pace. The scrubber can always rewind a beat and replay it as slowly as wanted.
- **Code card is a mirror, not a demand:** one or two lines, highlighted in sync with the animation (`x = nums[i]`, `L = L + 1`, `stack.append(x)`, `node = node.left`). The learner never types; the card just shows that the picture *is* the Python.

### How a Tour differs from a Problem level

| | Guided Tour | Problem level |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | none — pure understanding | solve / return correct answer |
| Failure | impossible (safe pokes, thunks) | verdict pass/fail, POWER brownout |
| Input | poke: steppers, toggles, sliders, drag | write/step logic, Run |
| Playback | tap/scrub, autoplay off | run the real tracer animation |
| Narration | caption bubble above the board, every beat | minimal; focus on code + verdict |
| Meters | only the relevant one lit; rest grayed | all live and graded |
| Chrome | no timer / verdict / Run | full grading chrome |

### Handoff into the first problem
The tour ends on the **same board** the learner just poked. The handoff card says, e.g., *"You just built the machine that solves Two Sum. Ready to drive it?"* On accept, the board stays put and the mode **swaps in the problem chrome**: the Solve goal appears, the TARGET/SOLVED chips light, the POWER meter un-grays, the code card becomes editable/steppable. Nothing about the substrate changes — the learner is not thrown at a new picture, they're handed the controls to the picture they already understand. Each tour's `feedsInto` names that exact first problem (arrays → linear scan/sum; two-pointers → Two Sum II; hashing → Contains Duplicate; stack → Valid Parentheses; graphs → Number of Islands).

## 4. What to build first

**Build `arrays-and-indices` first, then `pointers-cursors` (with the tiny `walking-the-tape` bridge tacked onto pointers).**

**Why these two, given two-pointers already animates:** the two-pointer demo is impressive but, to a true beginner, *meaningless without them* — it silently assumes he knows what an index is, what "value vs position" means, and that a robot is just a number. Arrays and pointers are the root of the entire dependency graph, they reuse the **exact existing widgets** (the `_TapePainter` crates, the teal `L` caret, the STEPS meter, the scrubber, the `_codeCard`) with **almost no new art**, and building them immediately makes the already-shipped two-pointer animation comprehensible. Highest foundational value, lowest build cost, and it de-risks the thing you've already built. Do *not* start with hashing, trees, or graphs — each needs a brand-new substrate (pigeonhole wall, hanging mobile, 2D board) and would blow the budget before the foundation exists.

**Exactly what the first Guided-Tour build contains:**

*The reusable Tour engine (minimum shared infra), built once here:*
- A caption bubble pinned above the board.
- Beat sequencing driven by the existing scrubber/frame counter, with autoplay disabled and tap-to-advance.
- A meter-dimming config (light only named meters, gray the rest).
- Chrome suppression flag (hide Run / verdict / timer / POWER).
- The jargon-gloss chip component and the one-word-per-object enforcement.
- A handoff card component that swaps tour-chrome → problem-chrome on the same board.

*The `arrays-and-indices` tour content (with all §2 fixes folded in):*
- **Board:** existing crates, sortedness gradient **off** (meaningless here), a **single** robot — the teal caret relabeled **READER**. Concrete count: **5 crates**, value big/bright, index small/gray beneath.
- **Beat 1 (meet):** lay down 5 crates; narration: *"a fixed row of crates; the row's length is locked — none are added or removed."* Gloss "index" and, on first plural use, "indices."
- **Beat 2 (the secret):** drop a faint **FRONT** tick at crate 0's left edge; *"the machine stores only ONE thing — where the front is."*
- **Beat 3 (the jump):** read a crate via a **dashed ruler** from FRONT; robot lands in one stroke, in-between crates never light; STEPS ticks **+1** — and this is where "step" is defined: *"a step is one piece of work; fewer steps = faster."* Repeat for crate 0 and the last crate: still +1 each.
- **Beat 4 (code bridge, before any confusion):** map `nums[3]` → "the crate at index 3"; *"the square brackets mean look up the box at this index; `nums` is the name of the whole row."* Light the `x = nums[i]` card in sync with the ruler; add *"L is just your Python `i`."*
- **Free-play sandbox:** drag READER onto any crate, watch STEPS click +1 every time regardless of distance; shove it past the end and hit the **bumper wall** thunk. No goal.
- **Confusion beat:** `nums[3]` is the 4th crate (counting from 0); in 5 crates the last is `nums[4]`, `nums[5]` is the wall; reading `nums[3]` gives the *value* inside (could be 99 or −7), not 3. Index small/gray, value big/bright keeps them visually split.
- **Handoff:** *"Reading one crate is instant. Next: what happens when you visit them ALL?"* → straight into the `walking-the-tape` bridge tour (same board, same single robot, STEPS now counting to N), which then sets up Big-O and, downstream, the first real array problem.

Ship those two tours plus the engine, retrofit the existing two-pointer demo to run inside the same Tour chrome (applying its §2 fixes — count *looks* 1-2-3, free-play first, "tape" vocabulary, goal stated up front), and you have a coherent beginning-to-first-problem slice on the lowest-cost substrate you already own.
